item.title: State Police Investigate Fatal Dog Mauling in Santa Rosa; Dogs’ Owner Charged
item.description:
SANTA ROSA, N.M. — A 73-year-old man died Friday after being attacked by two dogs outside his home on Tapia Road, and the dogs’ owner now faces a felony charge, the New Mexico State Police said.

The State Police Investigations Bureau is leading the inquiry into the Aug. 28 attack that killed Randy Wade. The Santa Rosa Police Department and State Police officers were the first to respond before bureau agents took over the case.

Investigators said Wade was outside his home when two dogs belonging to James Campbell, 52, attacked him near a shed. The attack was determined to be unprovoked.

Campbell and a woman were staying at Wade’s home at the time. According to investigators, the woman was outside when she witnessed the attack and called for Campbell, who was inside. Campbell came out and secured the dogs in an enclosure, then moved Wade to the front porch, where Wade was found to be deceased. The woman called 911.

During an interview with investigators, Campbell acknowledged that he knew his dogs had previously been deemed vicious. Investigators also learned the dogs, both pit bull mixes, had reportedly been involved in an earlier attack and had recently been released from an animal shelter.

Campbell has been charged with Dangerous Dog (Death of a Person), a third-degree felony under New Mexico law.

The investigation remains active, State Police said.

item.title: Area Volleyball Roundup: Lady Tigers Fall to Silver; Tularosa Picks Up First Win
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The Alamogordo Lady Tigers came up short at home Tuesday night, falling to Silver in straight sets, 25-19, 25-17, 25-21.

Silver controlled the tempo throughout the match, holding off every Alamogordo push. The Lady Tigers battled to keep the third set close but couldn’t string together enough points down the stretch to extend the match.

The loss drops Alamogordo to 1-2 on the young season. The Lady Tigers won’t have long to regroup — they head south this weekend to compete in the Jane Leupold Sweet 16 Tournament in Las Cruces on Friday and Saturday, where they’ll face a deep field of competition.

Tularosa Earns First Victory of the Season

The Tularosa Lady Cats notched their first win of the year, sweeping Socorro in three hard-fought sets, 26-24, 25-18, 26-24.

It wasn’t easy. Two of the three sets went to extra points, with Tularosa closing out both the first and third frames 26-24. The Lady Cats showed poise in the tight moments, finding a way to finish sets that could have gone either way.

Tularosa improves to 1-4 and will look to build momentum when it hosts Mescalero Apache next Tuesday.

Lady Chiefs Still Searching for First Win

Mescalero Apache dropped a four-set decision to Alamo Navajo, falling to 0-4 on the season.

The Lady Chiefs will get a chance to break into the win column this weekend at the Gateway Christian Tournament in Roswell, which runs Friday and Saturday, before traveling to Tularosa next week.

Cloudcroft Splits at Hatch Valley Tournament

The Cloudcroft Lady Bears went 1-1 at the Hatch Valley Tournament, evening their record at 3-3.

Cloudcroft opened with a straight-set loss to Cimarron, 25-18, 25-22, 25-23, in a match that tightened with every set — the Lady Bears fell just two points short in the final frame.

They responded emphatically in their second match, dismantling Reserve in three lopsided sets, 25-11, 25-17, 25-7. The Lady Bears’ serving and net play overwhelmed Reserve from the opening whistle, including a dominant 25-7 closing set.

Cloudcroft gets a quick rematch with Reserve on Friday, this time on the road.

item.title: From Parole Officer to the Bench: Lujan Grisham Appoints Joseph Cutts to Otero County Magistrate Court
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — A longtime New Mexico corrections officer is moving from supervising criminal cases to presiding over them after Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham appointed Joseph Cutts to the Otero County Magistrate Court.

Cutts will take over Division 2 following the resignation of Judge Albert R. Greene III. His appointment begins Sept. 12 and will last until the next general election.

The appointment caps an unusual path to the bench. Cutts defeated Greene, the incumbent, in the June 2 Republican primary, and Greene stepped down after the loss. Because no other candidates filed for the seat, Cutts will run unopposed in the Nov. 3 general election — meaning the governor’s appointment effectively installs him in a job voters had already signaled would be his.

The Division 2 race was one of only a handful of contested contests on Otero County’s primary ballot this year, in a county where Republican primaries are frequently decisive. Magistrate judges in New Mexico handle misdemeanor cases and preliminary hearings, serving as many residents’ first — and often only — point of contact with the court system.

Cutts brings more than a decade of criminal justice experience to the role, though from the enforcement side rather than the courtroom. He has served as a senior adult probation and parole officer with the New Mexico Corrections Department since 2012, supervising offenders after conviction. He also teaches criminal justice at New Mexico State University Alamogordo.

His academic credentials run through the same field. Cutts earned an Associate of Applied Science in criminal justice from NMSU Alamogordo, a bachelor’s degree in criminal justice from NMSU in Las Cruces, and a Master of Science in criminal justice from the University of Oklahoma.

Unlike district court judgeships, New Mexico magistrate judges are not required to be licensed attorneys in most jurisdictions, opening the bench to candidates with broader criminal justice backgrounds like Cutts. 

Greene’s departure ends a relatively short but effective tenure on the court. Greene had a respectable reputation as an attorney prior to his appointment. He was appointed to the Otero County bench by Lujan Grisham in 2023, filling a vacancy left by the resignation of Judge Michael Ryan Suggs. Before joining the magistrate court, Greene worked as a domestic relations hearing officer with the Twelfth Judicial District Court and as a senior Children’s Court attorney with the New Mexico Children, Youth and Families Department.

Cutts is expected to stand for the seat in the Nov. 3 general election, where he faces no opposition.

item.title: Eight Plein Air Artists to Open at Otero Artspace This Friday
item.description:
Alamogordo, NM — Otero Arts will open a new exhibition, “Eight Plein Air Artists,” with a public reception this Friday, September 4, from 5 to 7 p.m. at the Otero Artspace, 1118 Indiana Avenue at 12th Street.

The show features work by eight area painters: Anne Aleshire, Janet Amtmann, Lyn Canham, Rand Carlson, Deidre Kindthistle, Sue Nichols, Julie Ford Oliver, and Diana Powell. Their paintings were created on site at locations across the region, including Bent, Tularosa Falls, High Rolls, Alamogordo, La Luz, White Sands National Park, Nichols Ranch, and the Alamogordo Zoo. Media represented in the show include acrylic, oil, watercolor, pastel, and gouache.

Plein air painting — a portrait of the landscape in natural light — is a genre developed by painters in the 1800s who left their dark studios behind, carrying easels and tubes of paint outdoors.

Most of the artists in the show began painting together in October 2025 in a plein air workshop taught by Santa Fe artist Anita Louise West. Since then, the group has met one day a week to paint “en plein air.” Many have practiced the craft for years, painting throughout New Mexico as well as on trips abroad, in Alaska, and elsewhere.

Visitors to the exhibition will find anecdotes displayed alongside the paintings, describing what drew each artist to the subject of the piece. Kindthistle’s “The Pool,” for example, began as a tribute to David Hockney and became a farewell portrait: after 30 years of offering citizens a friendly respite from summer’s heat, the city pool is slated for demolition, to be replaced by a modern natatorium.

For Amtmann, who came to ranch life as a young woman, plein air painting is a way of preserving a quietly vanishing world. For decades she has painted what surrounds her in the Sacramento Mountains — the horses and cattle, the orchards and wildflowers, the storms and long evening light, and the people who make their lives on that ground.

“Eight Plein Air Artists” runs through September 26. The Otero Artspace gallery is open Thursday through Sunday, 1 to 4 p.m.

This October, Otero Arts will offer its fourth plein air workshop, again taught by Anita Louise West. Sign-up details are available at oteroarts.org. Anyone interested in joining the plein air painters on Thursdays may contact janet.amtmann@gmail.com.

The exhibit is supported by New Mexico Arts, the Department of Cultural Affairs, and the National Endowment for the Arts.

item.title: Changing the Narrative on Suicide’ brings walk, workshops and mayoral proclamation to Alameda Park Saturday
item.description:
Alamogordo N. M- Alamogordo residents will gather at Alameda Park this Saturday, Sept. 5, from 8 to 11 a.m. for “Changing the Narrative on Suicide,” a free community event offering a morning of movement, resources, and open conversation about suicide prevention.

Mayor Sharon McDonald will deliver remarks and an official proclamation, and speakers will share how suicide has affected their lives. An open space will give community members a chance to tell their own stories, and more than 13 local organizations — including 100% Otero and The Toy Train Depot — will be on hand with booths and resources.

Fitness instructors from around the community will lead free workshops throughout the morning. According to the schedule posted on the Chamber of Commerce’s community calendar, yoga begins at 8 a.m., followed by tai chi at 8:30, Zumba at 9, MixxedFit at 9:30, belly dancing at 10, and dance fitness at 10:30.

The event is hosted by the Otero Youth Empowerment Project and the Otero Humanists, whose co-founder and director, math and computer science tutor Spencer Bond, began organizing it about two months ago after losing someone close to him to suicide. What started as one person’s idea quickly grew into a citywide effort, with organizations, instructors, and volunteers signing on to help.

“Suicide prevention is so much bigger than any one of us,” Bond said. “This event never would have come together without the help of the community.”

Nani Lawrence, president of the Otero Humanists, helped shape the morning’s lineup of activities, with an emphasis on hope rather than heaviness.

“When you talk about suicide, it can be very much doom and gloom as it is,” Lawrence said. “However, our event focuses on the things that you look forward to that might make someone realize that they have all these great things. I think that it will provide a lot of hope.”

Organizers say the event is designed for everyone — those who have lost someone to suicide, those who have struggled themselves, and anyone who wants to support their neighbors. Families are welcome, and no registration is required.

“Changing the Narrative on Suicide” will be held Saturday, Sept. 5, from 8 to 11 a.m. at Alameda Park in Alamogordo. Admission is free. For more information, contact Spencer Bond at 575-339-4046.

If you or someone you know is struggling, free and confidential support is available 24/7 by calling or texting the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

item.title: Mayor McDonald Says Public Response to Bonito Lake Conversation ‘Remarkable’
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Facing an outpouring of public support for Bonito Lake, City Manager Brian Stockwell announced he will recommend a change of direction to the Alamogordo City Commission on Sept. 22 — one that keeps the lake open for fishing while regional talks explore its recreational future.

Stockwell made the commitment at a community forum hosted at Otero Arts by Alamogordo Town News and KALHRadio.org, which drew a large and diverse crowd of attendees, including elected leaders and city and county managers from across the region. More than 770 individuals have since watched the broadcast on YouTube. The full forum can be viewed at: https://www.youtube.com/live/MW0TxL89yQM?si=t9i-0zFcxKyKxlKh

McDonald: 'Your voices are being heard'

Alamogordo Mayor Sharon McDonald said the public response to the Bonito Lake issue has reached well beyond the city limits.

“The public response regarding Bonito Lake has been remarkable. I have received emails, calls, and text messages from people across New Mexico and as far away as Texas,” McDonald said. “Although I have not responded to everyone individually, I have read every email and reviewed every message. I want to respond collectively and assure you that your voices are being heard.”

“This is what meaningful citizen engagement looks like. Elected officials can serve most effectively when citizens speak up, share their concerns, and remain involved. I am proud of the respectful and passionate outreach from people who care deeply about Bonito Lake and its future.”

McDonald added that she “is encouraged by support from county officials and state legislators for keeping the lake open.”

“I will continue listening and working toward a responsible path that protects our water supply while preserving Bonito Lake’s important role in fishing, recreation, and family traditions,” she said. “Thank you to everyone who has reached out. Your involvement matters, and it is making a difference.”

A reversal, but not a retreat

Reading from prepared remarks — something he acknowledged he rarely does — Stockwell traced his history with the lake back to 1992, when he first managed the city and concluded that the lake’s role as the single best water source in the city’s inventory had to come before recreation. He noted the lake was already about 40 percent silted in during the 1990s, a problem that went unaddressed until the devastating 2023 fires and debris flows forced its closure. After restoration, water began flowing consistently to the city again in 2026.

Stockwell was at times defiant in defending his original recommendation to close the lake entirely, stressing that the detention basins, ponds, and drainage systems built to intercept debris have left surrounding areas hazardous. Former parking areas, he said, are now subject to mud flows that would have trapped vehicles during this summer’s storms. His comments returned again and again to a single theme: the lake was purchased in the 1950s as a water source, and protecting the city’s drinking water comes first.

But citing constructive public input and interest from state officials — including Sen. Townsend and the legislative representatives of the region, who have agreed to convene legislative colleagues and state agencies — Stockwell outlined five recommendations he will bring to the commission on Sept. 22:

1. Direct the city manager to open discussions with the state, Otero County, Lincoln County, and Ruidoso officials on options that preserve Alamogordo’s water supply while exploring compatible recreation at the lake and surrounding areas.

2. Continue construction of the remaining debris-flow protection projects.

3. Construct required security fencing around the dam structure and ancillary facilities only — not the lake itself.

4. Maintain the status quo allowing public access for fishing.

5. Post additional signage advising visitors that the lake is a primary municipal water source and that anyone entering city property does so at their own risk.

Stockwell also proposed a six-month deadline to report back to the commission on the results of the regional discussions.

A campaign promise in action

McDonald ran on a platform of supporting more transparency and getting people more involved in the conversation on a regional basis — one block at a time. A nongovernmental sponsored forum convening mayors from multiple cities in the region, alongside a dialogue with community members from across the area, reflects exactly that commitment to healthy debate and open governance — the kind of civic engagement that is the cornerstone of a vibrant and active local government in the region. Stay tuned for more updates and the public is still encouraged to attend the upcoming commission meeting and the one on Sept 22, 2026 to make public comment and keep the pressure ongoing.

item.title: In Memory of Evelyn Bernice Nowell Webb
item.description:
Evelyn Bernice Nowell Webb went home to her lord on August 27, 2026, at the age of 83.

Evelyn was born to Leon and Mary Nowell on November 17, 1942, in Alamogordo , New Mexico. She grew up in Tularosa and graduated from Tularosa High School in 1960. Later that same year, she married the love of her life, Dennis Webb.

Evelyn's love of adventure and travel began during her early years with Dennis.While he served in the Marine Corps, they lived in California, Arizona and North Carolina. Later in life Evelyn was blessed with the opportunity to see even more of the world. She visited 28 different countries an loved nothing more than sharing the stories and memories of her adventures with others.

Throughout her life, Evelyn wore many hats. She cleaned rooms, waited tables, worked as a telephone operator, and eventually retired from the State pf New Mrexico as an executive secretary. Whatever she was doing, she brought her own warmth, humor and personality to it.

Evelyn was a longtime member of the Tularosa Church of the Nazarene. When the Tularosa church closed, she became a member of Angus Church of the Nazarene. Her Faith was an important part of her life, and she faithfully served her church as a member of the church board, church secretary and treasurer.

Those who knew Evelyn will remember her wonderful sense of humor, her love of a good joke and a good giggle, and, most of all, her beautiful smile. She had a way of bringing joy and laugher to those around her. Her wit, humor and loving spirit will be deeply missed by all who had the privilege of knowing her.

Evelyn was preceded in death by her parents; three sisters; her brother; her husband, Dennis Webb; son, Dennis Webb Jr; and her daughter, Cheryl Parker.

She leaved behind to cherish her memory her son, Brandon Webb of Colorado Springs, CO; daughter, Beverly Brazel (Joe) of Capitan, NM; grandchildren, Keena Brazel of Capitan, New Mexico; Micharl Brazel (Janet) of Tucumcari, New Mexico; Cameron Parker of Tularosa, New Mexico; Dennis Webb (Samantha) of Spanaway, Washington; her beloved great-granddaughters, Avery, Adalynn and Willow Eve, who were the light and joy of her life; and her sister, Joyce Yearlt of Fort Collins, Colorado.

In lieu of flowers, Evelyn requested that donations be made to Bonita Park Campground.

A celebration of Evelyn's life will be held September 5, 2026, at 11:00 a.m. at Angus Church of the Nazarene, located at 103 Bonita Park, Angus, New Mexico. Lunch will follow at the same location.
The family has entrusted their loved one to the care of New Dawn Cremations for direct cremation.

item.title: In Memory of Virginia Chavez Estrada
item.description:
Life and Family
Virginia Chavez Estrada was called home by our Lord and Savior on Thursday, August 27, 2026. Virginia was born to Jose and Juanita Chavez on November 15, 1935. She was one of ten children.

Virginia was a devoted wife, mother, grandmother, great-grandmother, and great-great-grandmother whose greatest joy was her family. She is survived by her beloved husband, Pete Noriega Estrada, with whom she would have celebrated seventy-three years of marriage this November. She is also survived by her children: daughters Alicia Mancuso and spouse Paul Mancuso of Alamogordo, NM; Cecilia Estrada Ashe and spouse Michael J. Ashe of Chandler, AZ; and sons Estevan P. Estrada and spouse Renee Ankerstjerne of Lakeport, CA; Gilbert R. Estrada and spouse Elouise Estrada of Santa Fe, NM; Mario J. Estrada and spouse Juli A. Estrada; and Antonio L. Estrada. Virginia’s family was blessed with seventeen grandchildren, twenty-seven great-grandchildren, one great-great-grandchild, and many beloved nephews, nieces, cousins, and godchildren.

Virginia is also survived by her sisters, Patricia Padilla, whose spouse, Elijo Padilla, preceded her in death, and Lupe Maynez and spouse Oscar Maynez. She was preceded in death by her parents, her daughter, her grandson, two brothers, and six sisters.

Community and Service
Virginia was a dedicated community supporter who fundraised side by side with her husband for many organizations, including Sertoma Little League, Father James B. Hay School, the American Armed Forces Museum, and others. She also generously volunteered her time as a Zia Therapy Center board member for disabled children, at the Zia Therapy Center Thrift Store, Immaculate Conception Church, the Senior Citizens Center, the American Armed Forces Museum as secretary, and Father James B. Hay School as librarian.

Remembrance and Faith
Virginia worked for the Alamogordo Daily News and Alamogordo Credit Union. She will be lovingly remembered for her gift of making the best tamales, date cakes, and Mexican food, and for the warmth she shared with all who gathered around her table. Her life was rooted in unwavering faith, and her family takes comfort in knowing she is held high in the heavens. Her favorite quote was “Dios por delante y nosotros atrás de él,” translated as “God in front, we follow.”

Virginia’s legacy lives on through the family she cherished, the community she served, and the faith that guided her life.

The family is grateful for the love and support received during this difficult time. They are especially appreciative of the extended care given by Leticia Hawks, Stephanie Armijo Taylor, Amanda Mancuso, Margie Hernandez, and Virginia Simental.

Memorial Services
Memorial services will begin with the rosary and viewing on Friday, September 11, at 6:00 p.m. at Alamogordo Funeral Home, 2301 E. 1st Street, Alamogordo, NM. A Mass of Celebration will be held at 10:00 a.m. at Immaculate Conception Catholic Church, 705 Delaware Ave., Alamogordo, NM, with a reception to follow at Elks Lodge #1897, 2290 Hamilton Rd., Alamogordo, NM.

Paul bearers represented by her sisters and brother include Randy Pacheco, Christopher Pacheco, Rick Covarrubia, Raymond Telles, Frank Sierra, and Matthew Chavez. Honorary Paul bearers include Ramon Mancuso, Andrew Mancuso, Matthew Mancuso, Mario Estrada, Estevan Estrada, Anthony Ashe, Travis Bingham, and Aaron Estrada.

item.title: End of an Era: Triple Crown’s Departure Deepens Tourism Crisis From Ruidoso to Alamogordo
item.description:
RUIDOSO DOWNS, N.M. — September 4, 2026 — For 67 years, Labor Day in the Sacramento Mountains meant one thing: the thunder of quarter horses down the track at Ruidoso Downs, chasing the richest purse in the sport. Next year, that thunder moves to Texas — and with it goes the economic heartbeat of a region stretching from the Hondo Valley through Tularosa and down to Alamogordo.

Ruidoso Downs Race Track General Manager Rick Baugh announced Thursday that track owners Johnny and Jana Trotter have agreed on a framework with Global Gaming Solutions to relocate the Quarter Horse Racing Triple Crown Series — the $1 million Ruidoso Futurity, the $1 million Rainbow Futurity and the $3 million All American Futurity — along with the All-American Super Select Sale and the Ruidoso Downs Hall of Fame to Lone Star Park in Grand Prairie, Texas, beginning in 2027. The parties expect to finalize the agreement within weeks.

“This was not an easy decision, but we believe it is the right one,” Baugh said in a statement, citing the fires and floods of recent years as the catalyst for the move.

A Region Already Bleeding

The announcement lands on a region that has absorbed blow after blow since June 2024, when the South Fork and Salt fires burned roughly 17,000 acres and destroyed some 1,400 structures in and around the village of Ruidoso. The burn scars turned the mountainsides into runoff chutes, and the monsoon seasons of 2024 and 2025 brought repeated, destructive flash flooding. A July 2025 flood killed three people and sent the Rio Ruidoso surging past 20 feet — roughly five feet above the previous year’s high.

The racetrack, which sits along the river, sustained heavy damage. Officials canceled live racing at the facility and moved the meets to Albuquerque — first in 2024, then again for the entire 49-day 2026 season, including this year’s All American Futurity, scheduled for September 7 at The Downs at Albuquerque.

What was framed as a temporary relocation now becomes permanent for the track’s marquee institutions.

The Numbers Behind the Loss

The scale of the economic wound is hard to overstate for communities this size. Ruidoso Mayor Lynn Crawford has estimated the track generates $160 million to $180 million a year in revenue for the area — an enormous figure for a village of roughly 8,000 residents and its even smaller neighbor, the City of Ruidoso Downs, where more than a quarter of the workforce is employed in arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation and food service.

With the track dark this summer for a third year, Crawford has projected small businesses could see revenue drop 35 to 40 percent at the height of tourist season. The losses concentrate not just on race weekends but on weekdays, when owners, trainers, grooms and dedicated fans historically settled in for stays of three to four weeks at a time — filling cabins, RV parks, restaurants and shops in Midtown.

“It’s been kind of the lifeblood for the entire community,” Ruidoso Downs Mayor Carroll Scott told KRQE News after Thursday’s announcement, adding that the full impact on the surrounding Lincoln County communities remains unknown.

Ripples Down U.S. 70: Tularosa and Alamogordo

The pain does not stop at the Lincoln County line. Racing season has long spilled visitor dollars down U.S. Highway 70 into the Tularosa Basin. Horsemen boarded and trained animals at facilities such as Horseman’s Park in Tularosa, supporting feed stores, veterinary services, barn labor and agricultural suppliers. Race fans and industry workers who couldn’t find — or afford — lodging in Ruidoso routinely booked rooms in Alamogordo and Cloudcroft, fueling hotels, restaurants, gas stations and retail along the corridor.

Those seasonal jobs and that overflow spending were already diminished by three summers without racing. Thursday’s announcement converts a painful interruption into a structural loss. The trainers, the horse trailers, the August trial crowds, the Labor Day pilgrimage — the entire annual rhythm that moved money through Otero and Lincoln counties — now has a new address in the Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex.

What Remains

Ruidoso Downs officials have not detailed what future, if any, live racing has at the New Mexico facility once its signature events depart, though the Billy the Kid Casino and simulcast operations continue. Global Gaming Solutions, which operates Lone Star Park, said it is eager to bring the storied races and sale to North Texas fans.

For the mountain communities, the challenge now shifts to reinvention. The region still holds genuine draws — Ski Apache, the Lincoln National Forest, the Inn of the Mountain Gods, White Sands National Park to the south — and local leaders have pushed hard to market Ruidoso’s recovery. But none of those replaces a single Labor Day weekend that, for generations, put the region on the national map and tens of thousands of visitors in its beds, bars and shops.

The horses will run in 2027. They just won’t run here.

item.title: Alamogordo City Manager Performance Review Scheduled: Seventy Days In
item.description:
Alamogordo N.M. - On September 8, 2026, the Alamogordo City Commission will hold its regular meeting. One item deserves particular attention:

By September 8, City Manager Robert Stockwell will be in office for approximately 70 calendar days.

Seventy days is certainly not enough time to fully judge an administration. But it is enough time to begin evaluating direction: What has moved forward? What has stalled? How well is the public being informed? How are employees being led?

A performance review should not be viewed as an attack on a city manager. It is one of the Commission's most important responsibilities.

Bonito Lake: The First Major Test

One of Stockwell’s first significant policy recommendations involved Bonito Lake. On August 25, he recommended ending recreational access and proposed fencing that could have cost up to $1 million. The proposal generated substantial opposition from Alamogordo and surrounding communities. Following significant public engagement, Stockwell changed direction and announced that he would instead recommend maintaining fishing access while limiting fencing primarily to the dam area.

Changing direction after hearing from the public is not the problem. The problem is that r reporting by Alamogordo Town News identified a $250,000 legislative appropriation tied to reopening and day-use improvements, the existing Open Gate arrangement, negotiations for a multimillion-dollar project, and improvement work already underway. Those facts should have been part of the original recommendation and public discussion and were admitted to and confirmed by the city during the Voices of Alamogordo Community Forum not during the policy briefing to the commission and the public. This was a major error in informing the commission and the public about the true status of the lake. 

The lesson from Bonito is simple: the public should not have to challenge a recommendation before receiving the full picture.

Access and Communication

Stockwell also reopened portions of City Hall during the lunch hour. On its face, expanding public access sounds positive.

However, this outlet has received complaints that the utility billing/cashiering operation, the area many citizens actually use, remains unavailable until 1 p.m. If that is accurate, the change may not have solved the primary access problem for residents who need to conduct business during lunch.

That is the difference between changing hours and actually improving service. The performance review should ask whether the change produced any real benefit or whether it was simply smoke and mirrors, a visible change pushed by Commissioners Rardin and Hernandez, who had repeatedly called on the record for City Hall to remain open during lunch, while the primary public-facing service remained closed.

Communication is another concern.

During 2025 and the first half of 2026, residents regularly received project updates, department information and Commission presentations explaining what was happening across the City. That flow of information has slowed considerably.

At least two employees have told this outlet that managers should no longer speak during Commission meetings and that information is expected to come through department directors. But managers are often the employees working directly with projects and citizens and may have the most detailed operational knowledge.

The issue is not simply who speaks. The issue is whether information is reaching the Commission and the public, or whether there is a deliberate effort to stifle communication and control the flow of information.

What Happened to the Project Pipeline?

Stockwell did not inherit an empty project list.

Earlier this year, 2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News reported extensively on major water, sewer, road, public safety and recreation projects to be awarded to bid in 2026. On May 2, Dr. Hernandez reported that the City had completed 12 major projects, had approximately 20 more in progress and another eight ready to move forward. Project updates were again publicly presented at the May 26 Commission meeting.

When this outlet asked Hernandez about that project pipeline as she prepared to leave, she said, “Many were wrapping up and we had some major ones on deck”. The City also had significant financing identified, including the approximately $12 million natatorium financing and $28 million approved water and sewer funding.

When asked whether she intended to put additional projects out before leaving, Dr. Hernandez said:

“No. My focus is on wrapping up what I can and leaving the next round of projects to the incoming administration. There are several projects that are ready to go, with funding already identified, and simply need to be put out. My priority during my time as City Manager was to move forward projects that had been sidelined or delayed through the turnover in leadership. Every city manager brings a different perspective and may prioritize projects differently. From a professional and transition standpoint, I did not think it was appropriate to launch any major new initiatives without City Manager Stockwell’s input.”

The only public update we have seen has come from the Mayor’s Office. While that update said several major projects were expected to move forward, we have yet to see confirmation that they have actually been advertised or awarded. This outlet continues to monitor City bid postings and procurement activity, and the public record does not yet show the level of movement suggested in that update.

Many projects now appear delayed, yet there has been little public explanation, and seemingly little communication to the Commission, about why or when they will move forward.

That silence is creating another concern.

Some contractors have told this outlet they were not given an opportunity to bid on certain work. There is also concern that work could be directed to a contractor(s) with ties to Mayor Pro Tem Rardin. That allegation is not yet proven, which is exactly why the City should put the procurement record on the table: 

Who had an opportunity to bid? Who submitted proposals?
How was the contractor selected? 

And did any commissioner have involvement in the process?

If the process is clean, the records should show it. IPRA requests are pending on how awards were recently given to work that would normally go to the on call contractor. 

The Natatorium Deserves Clarity

The Natatorium raises another obvious question.

Sources have raised concerns that the City is considering spending approximately $1 million on outside project-management services, potentially using money otherwise available to construct the pool.

Why?

The City already has two project managers on staff. For more than a year, the Senior Project Manager successfully completed and kept numerous major capital projects moving while serving as the City’s primary project manager. A second project manager was hired earlier this year.

If that internal capacity already exists, why spend approximately $1 million on additional outside management instead of putting that money directly into the Natatorium?

That matters because the pool had already been scaled back to remain within approximately $12 million in available financing. If another $1 million is removed, what else gets cut? Features? Amenities? Improvements?

This outlet contacted former City Manager Hernandez regarding the issue. Her response was:

“At the time I left, the idea had been discussed, but nothing was finalized, and the initial cost estimate was extremely high. If another funding source could have been used instead of taking money from the pool, I would have supported it. But even with the $12 million loan, the pool design had already been scaled back, and I was not in favor of reducing it further. Any current updates should come from the City Manager Office or the Community Development Department that oversees this project”

Until the City explains whether an additional project-management contract is being pursued, what it will cost, why outside management is necessary when two project managers are already employed, and what funding source will pay for it, the question remains:

Why spend money managing the pool that could instead be spent building the pool?

Experience Comes With Expectations

Some will argue that Stockwell has only been City Manager for a little more than two months.

That argument only goes so far.

Mayor Pro Tem Rardin repeatedly emphasized Stockwell’s decades of city-management experience, his long association with ICMA and the fact that he previously served as Alamogordo City Manager. He was not presented as someone who needed months to learn municipal government or Alamogordo. His experience was part of the justification for hiring him.

So was his compensation.

Stockwell's base salary is $180,000. When the $6,000 vehicle allowance, retirement contributions, insurance, retiree-health contribution, ICMA membership and other employer-paid benefits are included, his estimated recurring compensation package is approximately $236,700 to $242,200 annually.

With that level of experience and compensation, the public should expect leadership, communication, project movement, organizational stability and informed recommendations.

Employee Leadership Matters Too

Employees inside City Hall have described increased tension and uncertainty. A transition can create discomfort, but transition cannot become a blanket excuse for an unhealthy working environment.

Former Mayor Payne summarized her concern this way:

“They are taking us back to a time when employees feared the commissioners. Being a commissioner meant walking into city hall and ordering staff and the city manger just sat in their office and did nothing to protect their employees. Following ICMA best practices, That’s not the way it’s supposed to work” 

Payne’s comments are especially relevant because this appears to be exactly the environment Mayor Pro Tem Rardin has wanted to restore, one where commissioners can exert direct influence inside City Hall, employees are reluctant to challenge them, and the City Manager does little to stop it.

That is precisely why the City Manager’s independence matters.

Some residents were concerned from the beginning that Stockwell’s appointment would make him more responsive to a four-member Commission majority than to the organization and broader community. Seventy days in, the pattern increasingly gives those concerns weight.

The question is whether Stockwell is acting as the professional barrier between politics and administration, or enabling the very culture Payne described.

Is he protecting the professional role of staff?

Is he providing complete information to all seven commissioners?
Is he maintaining meaningful communication with the public? 

And is he willing to tell commissioners no when their involvement crosses from policy into administration?

Those are City Manager questions.

Accountability Is Part of the Job

The September 8 performance review should not be about personalities or political sides.

It should be about measurable leadership.

Are funded projects moving?

Is the Commission receiving complete information before major recommendations are made?

Are citizens receiving regular updates?

Are changes at City Hall substantive or merely façade improvements?

Are employees being supported and allowed to provide their professional expertise?

And most importantly, is the City Manager providing the independent professional management Alamogordo is paying for?

The Commission hired the City Manager. Evaluating his performance is part of governing.

After approximately 70 days, there is enough of a record to start asking those questions.

The Final Question Is Transparency

The Commission is recessing into executive session, not adjourning the meeting. It will return to open session afterward.

Closed-session confidentiality does not require silence once they return.

Citizens can reasonably expect some indication of the outcome: Were expectations established? Were concerns addressed? What should the public expect going forward?

After 70 days of questions about communication, project direction and transparency, what happens when the Commission returns to open session may tell citizens just as much as what happens behind closed doors.

Will the Commission and City Manager provide a meaningful glimpse of where this administration is headed?

Or will they reconvene, say little, and once again leave the public with more questions than answers?

item.title: Organ Mountain Beats Alamogordo 27-0; Tigers Fall to 1-2
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The Alamogordo Tigers’ offense never found its footing this weekend on the road as Organ Mountain rolled to a 27-0 shutout victory, handing the Tigers their second straight loss and dropping them to 1-2 on the season.

The Knights struck first midway through the opening quarter when Enrique Ramirez connected with Michael McGill on a 25-yard touchdown pass. The extra point was good, and Organ Mountain carried a 7-0 lead into the second quarter.

Romeo Jones extended the advantage with a 9-yard touchdown run with 3:31 remaining in the first half. Though the extra point was blocked, the Knights took a 13-0 lead into the locker room at halftime.

Alamogordo’s hopes of a second-half comeback faded quickly. Jaden Gonzalez broke free for a 26-yard touchdown run with 6:07 left in the third quarter, pushing the lead to 19-0 after a failed two-point conversion.

Jones put the game out of reach in the fourth quarter, punching in his second score of the night on a 4-yard run with 5:57 to play. Kraft converted the two-point attempt to set the final margin at 27-0.

The shutout loss leaves the Tigers searching for answers on offense after failing to reach the end zone all night with several reported injuries as well. Alamogordo will look to bounce back when it hosts Roswell on Friday.

item.title: Animal Village NM Offering Affordable Spay and Neuter Surgeries for Low-Income Families
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Animal Village NM is once again opening its doors to low-income pet owners, offering affordable spay and neuter surgeries for dogs and cats belonging to families in Otero and Lincoln Counties.

Registration for the September clinic will take place Tuesday, September 8, from 11:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. at White Sands Mall. Families receiving Medicaid or EBT benefits qualify for the program, which provides surgery, a rabies vaccination, a microchip, and pain medication for a co-pay of just $65. Animal Village NM subsidizes approximately $200 per surgery to make the service accessible to those who need it most.

“This program is about more than preventing unwanted litters,” organizers say. “It’s about keeping pets in loving homes.”

More Than Just Surgery

What sets the program apart is its comprehensive approach to pet welfare. Beyond the operating table, participating families receive free training assistance from certified trainer Nathaniel Lucas, along with training tools to help address behavioral challenges — one of the leading reasons pets are surrendered to shelters.

Each pet also goes home with a gift bag containing post-operative care items, including an e-collar to protect the surgical site and a Kong toy to keep pets safely engaged during recovery.

Reducing Shelter Overpopulation

Spay and neuter programs like this one play a direct role in reducing the number of unwanted litters, easing intake pressure on local animal shelters and ultimately lowering euthanasia rates. By pairing affordable surgery with behavioral support, Animal Village NM aims to break the cycle of pet homelessness and abandonment in the region.

The organization has performed more than 11,000 surgeries over nearly 20 years of service to the community.

How to Qualify

Surgery spots are limited each month, and organizers encourage families to pre-qualify ahead of time. The process takes about two minutes and requires only Medicaid or EBT information and basic pet details. Pre-qualification is available online at AnimalVillageNM.com.

Families who qualify are urged to register early at Tuesday’s event to secure one of the limited surgery appointments.

item.title: Busy Weekend for Otero County Teams on the Pitch and the Court
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Otero County high school teams were in action across southern New Mexico over the weekend, with the Alamogordo boys soccer team capping a tough tournament run on a high note and area volleyball squads searching for answers after winless outings.

The Alamogordo boys soccer team ended the Roswell Coyote Classic in style, blanking Valencia 4-0 in its tournament finale. item.title: Jury Finds Ty Huntington Guilty of First-Degree Murder in Shooting Death of Mario Reyna
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — An Otero County jury has convicted Ty Huntington of first-degree murder and tampering with evidence in the December 2024 shooting death of Mario Reyna, 12th Judicial District Attorney Ryan Suggs announced Monday. The verdict was returned Friday, September 4, following a trial in Otero County.

The deadly encounter grew out of what prosecutors described as a dispute over a truck. Reyna had sold the vehicle to Huntington's family for $2,500, but the two sides disagreed over whether the full price had ever been paid. What began as a disagreement over money escalated into a back-and-forth struggle for possession of the truck — and ultimately ended in Reyna's death outside his own home.

A Dispute That Turned Deadly

According to the District Attorney's Office, the confrontation began on the evening of December 13, 2024, when Huntington and his stepmother took the truck while Reyna was at a Home Depot. During that encounter, prosecutors said, Huntington tried to provoke Reyna into a fight, and when Reyna refused, Huntington pulled a handgun and warned him not to interfere. Reyna reported the incident to law enforcement.

The next day, Reyna recovered the truck. He removed the stepmother's belongings, returned them to her, and told her she was free to contact police — adding that he would be at his home.

Roughly 45 minutes later, surveillance footage showed Huntington driving past Reyna's residence, apparently searching for the vehicle. After Reyna arrived home, neighborhood cameras captured Huntington pulling up in the same vehicle he had driven the night before at the Home Depot. Armed with a .45-caliber handgun, Huntington jumped Reyna's fence and entered the property.

Reyna came outside and confronted Huntington from his doorway. Prosecutors said Huntington declared he was taking the truck and once again tried to goad Reyna into fighting. When Reyna said he was calling the police, Huntington fired a single shot, striking Reyna in the abdomen, then fled the scene in Reyna's truck.

Officers and first responders attempted life-saving measures, but Reyna died at the scene.

Investigation and Arrest

The 12th Judicial District Major Crimes Unit — a multi-agency team drawing from the Alamogordo Police Department, Otero County Sheriff's Office, Lincoln County Sheriff's Office, and Ruidoso Police Department — took over the investigation. Huntington was located and arrested two days after the shooting without incident.

The case was prosecuted by District Attorney Ryan Suggs and Deputy District Attorney Melissa Garcia.

"This case is a tragic reminder of what can happen when someone chooses a firearm and violence to settle a dispute. No disagreement over money or property is worth a human life," Suggs said. "I want to thank the investigators of the Major Crimes Unit, our prosecutors, victim advocates, support staff, law enforcement officers, first responders, and everyone who worked tirelessly to bring this case to trial and seek justice for Mario Reyna and his family."

What Comes Next

Sentencing will be scheduled before Chief Judge Daniel A. Bryant. Huntington faces a life sentence for the murder conviction, along with additional potential penalties tied to the tampering-with-evidence conviction and his habitual-offender status.

The District Attorney's Office extended condolences to Reyna's family and loved ones and thanked the jurors for their service to Otero County and the justice system.

item.title: Residents Launch Accountability Push as City Commission Prepares to Review City Manager
item.description:
Almagordo — A growing group of residents is calling for greater accountability at City Hall, organizing around an upcoming performance review of City Manager Mr. Stockwell and voicing frustration with what they describe as an unresponsive majority on the city commission.

The effort, outlined in a recent community update delivered by local organizer Kim Great White Owl Murillo, centers on a newly created Facebook group, Almagordo Voters for Accountability, which aims to keep residents informed and encourage participation in local government.

Hear her own words at:

https://youtu.be/Mo7S2uTnU1w?is=T8zJJ0c9EM9jMQbK

Performance Review Set for September 8

The city commission scheduled and held an executive session closed door non-public on September 8 to evaluate Mr. Stockwell's performance. According to the update, the review was expected to examine his expertise, experience, and compensation and success to date. 

Organizers say the community's expectations are straightforward: strong leadership, transparent communication, measurable progress on funded projects, and respectful treatment of both city employees and residents. They argue the session should serve as a genuine assessment of leadership effectiveness rather than a procedural formality.

Bonita Lake at the Center of Criticism

Much of the group's criticism focuses on the handling of the Bonita Lake master plan. Members of the movement allege that the process suffered from inadequate public disclosure and claim that communications around the plan stoked unnecessary fear among residents. For many involved in the accountability effort, the lake has become a symbol of broader concerns about how major projects and natural resources are managed.

Beyond Bonita Lake, residents involved in the movement have raised a range of complaints, including delays on funded projects, unclear and incomplete public communication, restricted access to City Hall offices, and reports of low morale among city employees.

A Divided Commission

The update also points to a bloc of four commissioners whom organizers describe as unresponsive to public concerns. Supporters of the movement argue that this voting majority has marginalized community voices and contributed to a breakdown in trust between residents and their elected representatives.

Whether the criticism will translate into formal recall proceedings remains to be seen. Organizers have indicated that recall efforts are on the table if residents conclude that city leadership is failing to meet community needs.

"Not About Personal Attacks"

Movement leaders have been careful to frame the effort as one of stewardship rather than hostility. The goal, they say, is not to target individuals but to ensure responsible management of public resources — water, infrastructure, and tax dollars.

The call to action is simple: stay informed, show up, and speak out. With the September 8 executive session approaching, residents on both sides of the debate will be watching closely to see how the commission responds — and whether the accountability movement gains further momentum.

item.title: In Memory of Norman Lane
item.description:
Norman Lane, 93, passed away peacefully on September 6, 2026, in Las Cruces, New Mexico. Born and raised in Cloudcroft, New Mexico, he later made Alamogordo his home for 68 years, eventually moving to Las Cruces, NM for health care.

Norman proudly served in the United States Navy during the Korean War. After his military service, he built a successful career as a businessman and land developer. His ventures included Lane Plumbing Co., inc. in 1962, Lane Good Housekeeping Store, Desert Hills Subdivision and many others. He gave generously of his time to the community through his involvement with the Noon Lions Club, the Masonic Lodge, and the Elks Lodge. Norman is survived by his three children, Gary Lane (Wanda), Cheri Rabon (Randy), Debbie Moore; his seven grandchildren, Kayla Lane, Norman Jaret Lane (Katie), Kelsey Joy Lane, Kristy Alsleben (Matt), Chad Rabon (Paige), Cody Lane Craig (Nikki), Abe Moore (Juliett), Josh Moore (Christine); his 14 great grandchildren.

He leaves behind many special friends including his dear friend, Yvonne Brown, as well as countless lives he touched over the years.

item.title: In Memory of Lynne Ezelle
item.description:
On Easter Sunday, Lynne Ezelle was welcomed into Heaven by her beloved daughter Laura, her husband James “Donald”, and her very special brother, Jim — a reunion as full of grace as the life she lived.

Lynne was born on September 9, 1936, in Kittanning, Pennsylvania, to James McCoy and Georgia Morris. Her early years carried her from Detroit, Michigan, to Gadsden, Alabama, and eventually to Lakeland, Florida, where roots began to take hold. A cherished chapter of her youth was spent in Huntsville, Alabama, in the warm and loving home of Aunt Marion and "Doc" Caldwell.

A woman of beauty and taste, Lynne attended the University of Florida, where she majored in Interior Design within the School of Architecture. She was a proud member of Kappa Delta Sorority and was honored as a Sweetheart of the Delta Tau Delta fraternity. It was in those early Florida years that she met James “Donald” Ezelle. They married on December 23, 1952, shortly before her graduation, and began a life together that would be defined by creativity, faith, and devotion to family.

The couple settled in Melbourne, Florida, where they threw themselves into the life of their community. As charter members of Eastminster Presbyterian Church, they served on the building committee and took great pride in helping bring to life the stained glass windows that are still present in the sanctuary. They served as Youth Leaders, and later, Lynne returned to both Sunday School teaching and youth ministry as her own daughters grew in faith alongside her. Together, Lynne and Don also lent their considerable talents to the Brevard Civic Theater, where set design became another canvas for their shared creativity.

Lynne was a devoted and irreplaceable mother to her three daughters — Terri Lynne, Marion “Dawn” and Laura Ruth — and her love for them was the quiet, steady current beneath everything she did. When her youngest, Laura, was diagnosed with a brain tumor at just eight years old, Lynne met that heartbreak with extraordinary strength and tenderness. For years, she cared for Laura with tireless, selfless devotion until Laura's passing in 1994. That love never wavered, not for a single day. Through all of those responsibilities, she made sure that her girls never missed out on fun, taking trips all over the southern states in a Station Wagon or the Camper Van. Her daughters, in turn, loved their mother with a completeness that words can only begin to approach. She was their compass, their comfort, and their greatest champion — a woman whose lady-like demeanor never overshadowed her warmth, and whose strength never diminished her gentleness. To Terri and Dawn, she was simply the heart of the family, the keeper of its stories, and the standard by which love itself was measured – a true Matriarch.

When Don acquired the historic Glen Choga lodge in the mountains of North Carolina alongside dear friends from Melbourne, Lynne embraced the adventure with enthusiasm. While the men restored the exterior, she lovingly added her touches to the interior with the eye of the designer she had always been — scouring antique shops for quilts, china, and treasures that would give the old lodge its next, beautiful life. Over time, they became the sole owners and spent many years there. It was the place of many memories with family and
friends.

Lynne began making visits to New Mexico to be near both of her daughters and her six grandchildren, and eventually Alamogordo became home. There, she found new purpose and joy. She found her truest joy in her children and grandchildren. From rodeos to ballet recitals, from volleyball and basketball games from track meets to school awards ceremonies, Grammie was always there, always encouraging – their greatest fan.

Finding a church home at Grace Methodist, she sang with the Chancel Choir, worked in the Grace Food Pantry and every Saturday she gave her time faithfully at Shared Table, continuing until her health made it no longer possible. She was also a proud and active member of the Flickinger Center Guild, where she ushered and worked the concession stand with the same cheerful commitment she brought to everything.

Lynne is survived by her daughters, Terri Koehler (Richard) and Dawn Van Arnam (fiancé, Saben Lessentine); her beloved grandsons Trey Koehler (Hannah) of San Clemente, California, Tyler Koehler (Emily) of Holloman AFB, and Grayson Koehler of St. Louis, Missouri; and her cherished granddaughters Lynley Koehler, Ashtyn VanArnam, and Avery VanArnam, all of Alamogordo. She is also survived by her sister, Leslie, and sister-in-law, Darlene, both of Iron City, Georgia, as well as nieces Pamela, Carrie, Stacie, and Kelly, and a nephew, James (Buddy).

She was preceded in death by her parents, James and Georgia; her daughter, Laura; her husband, Don; and her dear brother, James Caldwell Morris.

The family wishes to extend their profound gratitude to Dr. Sandra Grummert and the compassionate team at Alamogordo Home Health and Hospice, including therapists Kristi and Rolando. Her caregivers, Beth, Lynnette, Jonie, and Chloe, helped keep her with us longer than we might have hoped and became cherished members of the family. Thank you, from the bottom of our hearts.

She was a woman who made every room more beautiful — and every life she touched, more full.
A true Southern Lady

item.title: PRC Overhauls Utility Complaint Process; Otero County Customers Face New Steps, Tighter Deadlines

The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission has announced a broad rewrite of its procedural rules, including significant changes to how customers pursue complaints against Public Service Company of New Mexico (PNM) and other regulated utilities.

The Commission announced the change September 8, following adoption of a Final Order on August 27. Administrative publication of the replacement rule remains pending.

What the New Rules Require

Under the adopted text, customers generally must first attempt to resolve a dispute directly with PNM before turning to the Commission. If that fails, they must complete the PRC's informal complaint process before filing a formal complaint. Exceptions are available for health and safety issues and for other good cause.

Once a customer files an informal complaint and the utility answers, PRC staff are expected to issue an investigation result within 60 days, though extensions are permitted.

From there, the clock runs quickly: customers have just 10 days after receiving the investigation result to request mediation, arbitration, or file a formal complaint.

The rules also provide an important protection during the process. PNM generally cannot disconnect service over the disputed issue while a complaint is pending, provided the customer continues paying all undisputed charges.

What It Means for Otero County

For Otero County customers challenging estimated bills or billing errors, the practical takeaways are straightforward: keep records showing you contacted PNM about the problem, and watch the escalation deadline closely. Missing the 10-day window after staff's investigation result could mean losing the chance to press the dispute further.

The order does not change PNM rates, and it does not determine that any recent bills were improper. It governs process — the path a dispute must follow — not the underlying outcome.

Background and Next Steps

The rewrite replaces procedures under the Commission's existing rules of procedure, which have long directed consumers through an informal complaint stage with the PRC's Consumer Relations Division before a formal complaint can be heard by the Commissioners. The new rules arrive the same year the Commission transitioned its filing system from eDocket to the new PRCe360 platform.

Parties seeking changes to the Final Order may file rehearing motions through September 28, with responses due October 2. Given a PRC that needs a legislative overhaul and appears deeply embedded with utilities instead of acting on behalf of consumers your comments to the PRC are needed. 

Customers with questions about the complaint process can contact the PRC's Consumer Relations Division at 1-888-427-5772 (1-888-4ASK-PRC). The Commission's announcement and the complete Final Order are available through the PRC's website and its PRCe360 docket system.

item.title: Alamogordo Commission Raises Golf Fees, Approves Liquor License Transfer and Tables Fire Station 2 Change Order After Paving Debate
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — The Alamogordo City Commission moved through a seven-item agenda in unanimous fashion Tuesday night, approving a golf course fee increase, signing off on the transfer of an Albuquerque liquor license to a new North White Sands Boulevard dispensary, and lifting the condemnation on three properties — but the sharpest exchange of the evening came over a third change order on the Fire Station No. 2 project, which commissioners tabled until Sept. 22 after learning the trucks the station was built to house could not sit on the asphalt pad that had been planned for them.

The meeting, held at 6:30 p.m. in the Donald E. Carroll Commission Chambers at City Hall, was called to order by Mayor Sharon McDonald with all seven members present: Mayor Pro Tem Josh Rardin and Commissioners Baxter Pattillo, Stephen Burnett, Warren Robinson, Al Hernandez and Mark Tapley. Commissioner Robinson delivered the invocation and Commissioner Burnett led the Pledge of Allegiance. Every vote of the night was 7-0. The commission then adjourned into executive closed session under the Open Meetings Act to conduct City Manager Robert Stockwell’s performance review, and no further public action was taken.

Community Development Director Shelley Dowhanik-Baron and Fire Chief Ramirez presented Change Order No. 3 to National Construction’s contract for Fire Station No. 2, priced at $143,368.79. The largest piece swaps asphalt for concrete on the apron immediately in front of the apparatus bay doors. Dowhanik-Baron told commissioners she halted that portion of the work after a site visit several weeks ago when she saw the pad was scheduled to be asphalted.

Chief Ramirez said the Class A pumpers the city intends to park in the bays weigh roughly 75,000 pounds. He described what happened at Fire Stations 1, 5 and 6, which were built with asphalt in the early 2000s: the heavier trucks left indentations, water pooled in the ruts, and at Station 5 the pressure from ladder trucks ruptured a main water line running beneath the pavement. Those stations were eventually torn out and replaced with six to eight inches of concrete.

The change order also proposes asphalting the driveways around the building — surfaces Dowhanik-Baron said date to 1970 and are “really not asphalt” but dirt and rock that vehicles sink into during monsoon season — along with relocating exterior patio lighting to the building and tinting the windows of the firefighters’ living quarters for privacy.

Commissioner Burnett pressed on whether three inches of asphalt on the driveways would hold up any better than the pad, noting that on a 110-degree day a heavy truck can groove asphalt quickly. “I would prefer if we have to do it one time instead of two or three years down the road, we’re right back here at the same situation,” he said, asking whether the whole approach should be concrete from the street to the rear exit.

Commissioner Hernandez asked why, given the city’s own experience at its other stations, the issue was not addressed before the project went to bid. “Who was the engineer and the architect on this project? And did city staff not meet with them to discuss these issues prior to this going out to bid?” he asked. Dowhanik-Baron said the decision predated her tenure and that the project manager at the time chose to phase the work — building and adjacent pads first, driveways later — but she could not explain why the bay apron was not specified as concrete from the start.

“This is going to nickel and dime us to death on this,” Hernandez said, recalling that the first change order for the bay doors was likewise not in the original bid.

“I think this project is a prime example of what will never happen again. The idea of doing it piecemeal, the idea of not gathering all of the input from the department as the project went through the design phases — those are the mistakes that were made.”

— City Manager Robert Stockwell

Stockwell interjected to take responsibility for the process going forward, telling the commission that future projects will not be brought forward for bid award until the department has signed off on a complete design. He agreed with Burnett that concrete “from the street all the way around the building back to the exit” is the right answer, and said dead trees around the site — which he said should have been part of the original design — will be removed.

On funding, Stockwell said the original grant of $423,000 was spent early in the project and the remainder, including this change order, comes from Fund 69. Commissioner Tapley put the total project cost at roughly $1.3 million with the third change order. Asked for a ballpark on full concrete, Stockwell said he would be guessing but estimated a change order of $500,000 to $600,000 — at which point Tapley said the item should come back with a firm number. Dowhanik-Baron said the building itself is due for completion between Sept. 14 and 17, but Chief Ramirez noted apparatus cannot be moved into the bays until the apron is poured, and the added concrete and paving could push completion to mid-October.

Mayor McDonald asked whether Stockwell’s pledge meant projects would not be awarded at all when the city cannot fund the complete scope. “If we don’t have the money to do it, then we won’t bring it to you,” Stockwell replied. “That’s what I wanted to hear,” the mayor said. Stockwell also recommended that future project budgets carry a contingency line, which he said the city has not been doing.

On a motion by Rardin, seconded by Burnett, the commission tabled the change order to its Sept. 22 meeting, when staff is to return with a firm cost for concrete drive surfaces. Dowhanik-Baron told the commission she does not anticipate further change orders on the project.

Stockwell presented a fee increase for the municipal golf course, telling commissioners the cost of play across the region has risen significantly and the proposed schedule, based on a survey of surrounding courses compiled by the course’s management contractor, would place Alamogordo “not at the top, but not at the bottom either.” He framed the increase as groundwork for the long-term operation of the course and a stronger financial footing. Specific fee amounts were not read into the record during the presentation.

Mayor McDonald asked the golfers on the dais whether they had fielded any calls about the increase. None had. “We probably will tomorrow,” Pattillo said before moving approval, which passed on a second from Rardin.

In the evening’s lone public hearing, the commission considered whether the state Alcoholic Beverage Control Division should approve a transfer of ownership and location for dispenser license DIS000927 to Sips on 6th LLC, with on-premises consumption and patio service, at 523 N. White Sands Blvd. The license is currently held in Albuquerque. Staff confirmed the notice was published twice, with the first publication at least 30 days before the hearing, and that the nearest church is more than 1,000 feet away — well beyond the state’s 300-foot rule. A representative for the applicant was present but was not called on. Hernandez moved approval, Tapley seconded, and it passed 7-0.

Robinson afterward asked whether the 300-foot church rule is still enforced, recalling that during his prior service on the commission roughly two decades ago a license was issued to the Allsup’s at 10th Street and Scenic Drive on the strength of a letter from the church’s pastor. “My concern was, what happens when that pastor moves or changes? Do they pull that license?” he asked. Staff said the distance requirement remains a state rule on the application.

Dowhanik-Baron, joined by Bohannan Huston planner Liz Treat, briefed the commission on the city’s new comprehensive plan, a 20-year visioning study awarded under the firm’s on-call task order for $144,578.16. Work began in June and is expected to run about a year, with a final report and actionable project list targeted for roughly June 2027.

The steering committee draws on department heads for fire, police, parks, community services, finance, public works and utilities, the city manager, and two outside members: Josh Ramsey, owner of the area’s McDonald’s restaurants, and Tom Furman, housing director for the Sacramento Mountains Foundation. Dowhanik-Baron said that based on gross receipts data, Ramsey’s restaurants feed roughly 20 percent of Otero County’s population in a given week.

Early census work shows Alamogordo has a larger share of residents aged 18 to 34 than anywhere else in New Mexico — a function of Holloman Air Force Base — alongside 22 percent under 18 and roughly 20 percent 65 and older. “So we’ve got those two polar ends of our demographics,” she said, pointing to affordable housing, workforce development and services accessible across age groups as planning priorities.

“We want brutal honesty. We don’t want fluff. Tell us the honest truth. What’s wrong with Alamogordo? What needs to be fixed? What’s right about Alamogordo? What do we treasure?”

— Community Development Director Shelley Dowhanik-Baron

Public input is being gathered through the Let’s Grow Alamo website, which hosts a community survey and an interactive map where residents can pin comments to specific parts of the city; a booth at Washington Park on the last Friday of August; printed surveys distributed at the meeting; and planned virtual focus groups with business, school and community stakeholders. Dowhanik-Baron asked commissioners to share the site on social media and said a facilitated work session with the commission is planned within the next six months. The transportation management plan being prepared by Lee Engineering and utility data on water and wastewater will feed into the study through GIS.

She distinguished this effort from prior plans — one in the late 1990s, one in 2011 and one around 2020 — by promising a documented pipeline of projects with cost estimates and schedules that can be carried directly to state and federal funders such as CDBG. “A lot of people think this is just a study that sits on a shelf and gathers dust,” she said.

Mayor McDonald asked a series of questions: whether the Chamber of Commerce is engaged (yes); whether the census figures reflect updated American Community Survey data rather than the 2020 count (updated); what role the Mayor’s Youth Advisory Commission will play (staff will present to the group and gather youth input on retaining young families); and how the plan squares with the city’s $160 million, 10-year infrastructure commitment. Dowhanik-Baron said the administration is building a five-year capital plan, extended to 10 years, as the specific prioritization tool, while the comprehensive plan sits above it as a broader visioning document. She also confirmed that the Sacramento Mountains Foundation’s housing plan and the Lakota housing study have been provided to Bohannan Huston for incorporation, and that the city is working through how it can lawfully partner with the foundation, since municipal funds cannot go to residents directly.

Code Enforcement Manager Josh Sides, appearing with Ryan Glidden of the police department, presented Resolution 2026-34 declaring three previously condemned properties no longer ruined, damaged or dilapidated: the Tinsley Trailer Park at 1620 N. White Sands Blvd., 801 Arapahoe Trail and 1803 College Ave. Sides said the violations cited at the trailer park in 2023-2024 have been corrected and that the two houses have been fully remodeled inside and out. JV One Tree LLC purchased the properties, he said, and both homes were subsequently sold after the work was complete. Robinson, who said he had seen 801 Arapahoe Trail in person, offered “kudos,” moved approval, and Hernandez seconded.

Tapley asked Sides about a home on Cuba Avenue the commission condemned earlier this summer, noting a for-sale sign has since appeared. Sides said the owner, a Mr. Braswell, is not deceased as he had initially believed but is incapacitated, and the courts have appointed an executor. He has mailed the resolution to the owner’s last known address and the listing brokerage, posted the property, and intends to contact the real estate office locally if he does not hear back soon.

Interim Parks and Recreation Director Heather Casebolt presented two on-call bid awards for commercial lawn equipment repair: IFB 2026-005 to Gary Childress for the Parks Department and IFB 2026-006 to CT Custom Services for the golf course. Casebolt said Childress, who is retired, worked heavily for Parks last year, while the golf course position had gone unfilled and has equipment such as the bunker rake out of service. Neither contract is capped, but Parks has budgeted $150,000 and the golf course $100,000. A commissioner asked why one tabulation listed only a $90-per-hour labor rate while the other included emergency and travel charges; Casebolt attributed it to Childress’s limited availability. Commissioners complimented the condition of the park turf and said the golf course is “looking pretty good too.” Rardin moved approval of both awards; Hernandez seconded.

The only public comment came from Johnny Powell of the New Mexico Museum of Space History’s Space Hall of Fame Foundation, who thanked the commission and announced the museum’s 50th anniversary celebration on Oct. 3 at the Tays Center, which will include the first Hall of Fame induction since 2016. Powell said he recently attended the Aerospace States Association conference, where states described space commissions ranging from a $600 million operation to a single staffer, and said New Mexico is developing its own. He said he hopes the foundation can represent Alamogordo, the Tularosa Basin and White Sands as that effort takes shape. Powell finished under his three minutes.

Stockwell reported on a meeting with a deputy regional forester for the U.S. Forest Service, following up on the commission’s resolution of support for the Sunspot observatory site. He said the mercury contamination inside the large solar telescope proved far more extensive than first thought: pooled mercury was removed, but it had migrated into the interior concrete of the structure and the telescope itself, which he was told extends 150 feet above ground and 250 feet below. Contaminated materials are being disposed of as the operating agency, whose name Stockwell said he could not recall, winds down the facility.

The Forest Service is working with the Sunspot community group on alternative uses, including the dark-skies designation the group has sought. Stockwell said that at minimum the roads, electrical and water systems will remain in place, and the agency’s stated intent is to keep the site an active, publicly accessible facility, though its future design and operation are undecided. No commissioner offered remarks or inquiries when the mayor opened that agenda item.

The final agenda item was a closed session under NMSA 1978, Section 10-15-1, for limited personnel matters — specifically the city manager’s performance review. City Clerk staff corrected the item on the record from “recess” to “adjourn” into executive session, meaning the public portion of the meeting ended with the 7-0 vote to close the doors. Hernandez moved and Rardin seconded. Any action arising from the review would have to be taken at a subsequent open meeting.

The commission’s next regular meeting is Tuesday, Sept. 22, at 6:30 p.m. at City Hall, 1376 E. Ninth St., where the Fire Station No. 2 change order is scheduled to return with revised concrete costs.
