item.title: Tularosa Planning and Zoning Grills Cell Tower Applicant, Advances Lot Split and Vacant Building Ordinance
item.description:
TULAROSA, N.M. — Sept. 8, 2026 — The Village of Tularosa Planning and Zoning Commission spent the bulk of its Tuesday meeting putting a proposed cell tower under the microscope, with one commissioner delivering a line of questioning so exhaustive that the applicant said he had never seen anything like it in hundreds of hearings.

Cell tower reapplication faces detailed scrutiny

The commission reviewed a reapplication from Flagship One LLC for a cell tower at 44 Sunset. Rather than voting on the project, the commission will issue findings of fact to the Village Council, which is responsible for scheduling and holding the required public hearing. Certified notices will be mailed to roughly 10 to 12 nearby property owners once a hearing date is set.

Company representative Sean Milks told commissioners the tower has been lowered from approximately 199 feet to 190 feet and repositioned so it now sits about 200 feet from all property lines — more than a one-to-one setback — meaning that even in a worst-case collapse it would not land on neighboring property. The tower is engineered to hold up to four wireless carriers, with Verizon as the anchor tenant at the top and space potentially available below 150 feet for municipal or public safety use at free or nominal rent.

Commissioner Bucky Johnson pressed Milks on a long list of technical and legal points, noting that because the village has no wireless ordinance yet, "I have to go question for question." Among the issues raised:

• Decommissioning: How the village would know if the tower "goes dark," and the terms of the removal bond. Milks said a submeter visible from outside the compound would show whether the site is drawing power, and that the removal obligation would be backed by a surety bond, with removal costs borne by his company, not the landowner. He also agreed to provide an annual written certification that the tower remains in active use.

• Engineering standards: Milks said the tower is designed to ANSI/TIA-222 Revision G and the 2025 New Mexico building code as a Risk Category 2 structure, with stamped manufacturer drawings to come. Johnson questioned whether adding municipal or emergency communications equipment would push the tower into Risk Category 3, with higher wind and ice factors; Milks said it typically would not, but that a certified New Mexico engineer would rerun the structural analysis before any new equipment is added.

• Outstanding studies: A geotechnical soils report is still in process, as is the NEPA and Section 106 State Historic Preservation Office review — a concern given Tularosa's historic district. Milks said he has hired the firm TriLeaf to complete that review and expects the roughly 140-page report within about 30 days.

• Site conditions: The site would be served by a dirt access road and visited only about once a month or every two months. Johnson pushed for dust and erosion control, suggesting hydroseeding around the foundation — a condition Milks said he had never been asked for before but would accept. There is no backup generator planned; carriers would rely on 8 to 10 hours of battery backup, and any future fuel tank would require village approval.

• Liability: Johnson sought assurance that the village would be indemnified against claims arising from the tower.

Because several reports remain outstanding, the commission agreed to make its recommendation conditional, with all required documents to be provided before a state building permit application can proceed through the New Mexico Construction Industries Division.

"That was thorough and you are doing your job," Chairwoman Hilton told Johnson. Milks agreed: "I've been in hundreds of these hearings and I don't think I've ever had someone go through it so thorough."

Two-lot split approved

In the meeting's only vote on an action item, the commission unanimously approved a two-lot split for Nancy Carr at Riata Road. Carr had withdrawn an earlier subdivision request in favor of the simpler split. Commissioners noted the property cannot be split again for five years, though they believed that restriction would not carry over to a future buyer.

Vacant building ordinance moves ahead

Commissioners spoke favorably of a proposed vacant building registration and maintenance ordinance now in the village's hands, along with a unified fee schedule, both part of a broader 2026 planning and zoning reform effort. The commission voiced frustration that attorney review of its proposed changes has dragged well past an expected 90-day window and asked staff to find out where the documents stand. Because the vacant building measure is a new ordinance and the fee schedule adjusts fees, both may require public hearings.

Johnson said he has already completed a property-by-property survey of problem parcels — covering the original 49 blocks and the area from 8th Street back to West Street — but noted that citations must go through the village's lone code enforcement officer. "I know you can't eat an elephant in one bite, but you can damn sure eat it a bite at a time," he said, suggesting the work be tackled section by section.

Commissioners also floated giving residents advance notice before code enforcement sweeps a street and reviving a spring cleanup with community dumpsters.

Abatement case stalls

On unfinished business, commissioners revisited a long-running nuisance abatement case involving a property connected to Carolina and Felipe Bermudez Marino. Officials said the property owner remains incarcerated and that the village has been waiting for the court to appoint a guardian ad litem before proceeding with cleanup. Some commissioners argued the village can legally act now and should, describing the property as a fire hazard. The matter will be placed on the next village meeting agenda.

The meeting was adjourned following a motion by Johnson, seconded by Commissioner Stephanie Dubois. Approval of the previous meeting's minutes was tabled.

item.title: PDGA TD Academy Disc-O-Zozo Classic
item.description:
Disc-O-Zozo Classic Comes to Carrizozo September 19

[Carrizozo, New Mexico, September 10, 2026] A PDGA C-Tier sanctioned disc golf tournament will take place Sept. 19, 2026 in Carrizozo, New Mexico. The one-day tournament is open to all players. As an entry-level event, beginners are eligible to play alongside experienced players. Both are able to earn official player ratings and points and player packs will be distributed. William Garrison is the event coordinator. Mr. Garrison recently graduated from the PDGA TD Academy, an in-depth management training program for members interested in running a PDGA C-Tier event.

Disc-O-Zozo was designed by Everett Brophy and takes advantage of the high plains terrain. Located just east of Carrizozo on US 380, the 18-hole course is relatively flat. It has a water feature but the most challenging aspect is usually the wind. September’s average wind speed is 11.5 mph, according to https://wanderlog.com.

“Carrizozo Works, Inc., a local not-for-profit, worked with the town administration to bring disc golf to Carrizozo three years ago” Lisa Maue, director of CWI said. “Since then we have hosted several tournaments. We are excited about this event and that William is the coordinator. A lot of people have worked hard to make Ruidoso an epicenter for disc golf, and we believe that Disc-O-Zozo complements the courses up the mountain in terrain, difficulty and accessibility. September is traditionally a perfect time as far as weather is concerned, and there are so many places to explore in and around Carrizozo. We hope players and their families will come and make a weekend of it.”

Registration is open to both current PDGA members and non-members. Players can register online at Disc Golf Scene. Spots are limited and early registration is recommended.

For more information, please contact William Garrison at (505) 426-6020.

US 380, just east of Carrizozo

item.title: From Meme to Microphone: Trump Floats Renaming New Mexico 'New America' at GOP Midterm Convention
item.description:
DALLAS — What began as a debunked internet hoax became a line in a presidential speech Wednesday night, when President Donald Trump told the Republican Party's first-ever midterm convention that New Mexico should be renamed "New America."

Speaking at the American Airlines Center on the convention's opening night, Trump raised the idea alongside other geographic renamings he has pursued, including the Gulf of America and Lake America.

"We did come up with one the other day which we think is appropriate," Trump said, according to Paul Sanchez, a New Mexico Republican and radio host who has tracked the controversy since it began. "You have a neighboring state, New Mexico. We think it should be called 'New America.'" Trump added that "the people love the idea."

National outlets confirmed the substance of the remarks. Yahoo News reported that Trump told the convention he was planning on renaming New Mexico "New America," and said the Strait of Hormuz would become the "Trump Strait" after the war with Iran.

A hoax that became real

The episode has an unusual origin. A false claim that Trump had signed an executive order renaming New Mexico circulated online — a recycled hoax dating back to 2016. Then, on Sunday, Sept. 6, Trump posted a map of the state on Truth Social with "Mexico" crossed out in red and replaced with "America." The official White House account reshared the image on X.

Trump followed with an AI-generated video of himself pasting an "America" sticker over a "Welcome to New Mexico" road sign, and by Labor Day had posted at least seven times about the proposal in roughly an hour, according to Forbes. In one post, he called New Mexico "one of the great vote cheating states" and said the new name would be more prestigious.

The White House has not announced any formal effort to rename the state, and as of this week no executive order had been signed.

The legal wall

Whatever the president's intentions, renaming a state is not within his power. While Trump can direct the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to change how the federal government refers to bodies of water — as he did with the Gulf of Mexico in January 2025 and Lake Ontario on Aug. 27 — states control their own names.

New Mexico's constitution states plainly: "The name of this state is New Mexico." Changing it would require action within the state itself, likely a constitutional amendment. No such process is underway.

Reaction across the spectrum

New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, a Democrat, rejected the idea outright, saying the state's name "isn't up for debate" and has belonged to the region since before the United States existed. She accused the president of using the stunt to distract from the war in Iran and rising prices. Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich and Ben Ray Luján also pushed back. Local Independent candidate for District 51 State Representative, Grace Nagamine posted a video questioning rather the president was serious or rather it was a joke but more importantly questioned why her opponent, John Block, was pushing the narrative via his social media posts.   She emphasized that “the rhetoric is divisive and we should be discussing the bread and butter issues that impact our local district, high electric prices, high gas prices, roads needing repairs and CYFD reforms, not renaming New Mexico. “

Some Republicans embraced the proposal — Utah Sen. Mike Lee called the name "kind of catchy" — while others in the party have grown uneasy with the convention's broader promises. Rep John Block supported the idea that dismisses the heritage of New Mexico and its history, he then later endorsed the narrative that it’s Trump trolling Democrats and individuals. Regardless it’s divisive and political leaders should unite individuals not divide. 

Chief among those new ideas Trump is now championing in what opponents claim is desperation that congress will never approve, Trump's pledge that every adult American citizen would receive a $5,000 "Trump Dividend" if Republicans hold the House and Senate in November — a proposal analysts estimate would cost more than $1 trillion and which critics note may run afoul of federal law against paying to influence votes. Texas Gov. Ron DeSantis denounced the plan, warning it would fuel debt and inflation.

'Which parts should we laugh at?'

For local commentator and Republican activist Sanchez, a self-described Trump supporter on issues from Iran to women's sports, the convention speech ended the debate over whether the president was joking.

When the Truth Social posts first appeared, he says, Republicans in New Mexico split into three camps: those who insisted it was a hoax, those who loved the idea, and those who said Trump was merely trolling the state's Democrats. Sanchez had leaned toward taking the president seriously — then conceded on air that it was probably a joke, only to watch Trump repeat the proposal from the convention stage a day later.

"The problem now is if you still go with the trolling line," Sanchez wrote, "please tell me what parts of the speech are jokes? The 5K? New America? Trump Strait?"

For now, "New America" remains a proposal without a process — a name change no president can make alone, aimed at a state that has already said no and yet another divisive policy in a time when unity and civility is truly needed. 

One correction is needed in the “New America” story: Ron deSantis is the governor of Florida, Greg Abbott is the Texas governor.

item.title: Twenty-Five Years Later: Timberon and Alamogordo Remembers 9/11
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — A quarter century after the September 11 attacks, the communities of the Tularosa Basin and Sacramento Mountains are pausing to remember — from the flats of Alamogordo and Tularosa to the forested canyon community of Timberon.

Friday, September 11, 2026, marks 25 years since 2,983 men, women, and children were killed in the attacks on the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and aboard United Flight 93 — a toll that includes the victims of the 1993 World Trade Center bombing memorialized alongside them. In New York, families gathered at the National September 11 Memorial plaza at 8:30 a.m. Eastern to read the names aloud, observing seven moments of silence — a new, seventh pause added this year to honor the more than 9,000 people who have since died of 9/11-related illnesses, nearly three times the number killed on the day itself.

President Trump marked the anniversary at the Pentagon, while Vice President JD Vance joined former presidents Obama, Bush, Clinton, and Biden at Ground Zero. But as in every year since 2001, the most personal acts of remembrance happened far from the cameras — in small towns like ours.

Alamogordo: Climb the Cube

The centerpiece of Otero County's commemoration comes Saturday, September 12, when the New Mexico Museum of Space History and the Alamogordo Fire Department host Climb the Cube: 9/11 Memorial Stair Climb at the museum, 3198 State Route 2001.

Registration opens at 7:30 a.m., and participants will be staggered into the climb beginning at 8:46 a.m. — the minute American Airlines Flight 11 struck the North Tower. Climbers will complete 12 circuits of the museum's iconic golden cube, representing the 110 flights of stairs in the Twin Towers, joining a nationwide stair-climb tradition honoring the 343 New York firefighters who ascended into the burning buildings and never came down.

The event is family-friendly and open to everyone — residents, first responders, businesses, schools, and community organizations are encouraged to climb individually or form teams. Advance registration is available at SpaceTrail.org/sites/StairClimb, with day-of registration starting at 7:30 a.m. As a thank-you, first responders and their immediate families receive free museum admission from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on September 12.

For a community that lives alongside Holloman Air Force Base and sent its sons and daughters into two decades of war that began that September morning, the climb is more than exercise. Every step is a name.

Timberon: Remembrance in the high country

Tucked into Sacramento Canyon at 7,000 feet, Timberon is a community of a few hundred souls served entirely by volunteers. The Timberon Volunteer Fire Department, organized in 1974 and operating today from its new station on Merlin Drive, is the beating heart of the community — which gives September 11 a particular weight in a place where every firefighter is a neighbor.

For volunteer departments like Timberon's, the anniversary of the day 343 firefighters died doing the job is felt keenly. Residents can check with the fire department — which meets the first Thursday of each month at 6:30 p.m. at the station — or the Timberon community calendar at timberon.org for local observances, and are welcome at the Alamogordo stair climb, where teams from across Otero County are invited to participate.

Why we still gather

Twenty-five years is long enough that a generation of Otero County students has no memory of the day. It is why organizers of the national commemoration added the seventh moment of silence, why the museum climb invites schools to send teams, and why small towns keep showing up year after year — at fire stations, on courthouse lawns, on museum stairs in the high desert.

The towers fell over2,000 miles from the Tularosa Basin. The obligation to remember did not.

Once the wrestlers clear the ring, the stage belongs to local performers. Food trucks, merchandise vendors, and a DJ will round out the festival atmosphere.

The night closes with a tribute to one of Mexico's most beloved icons: Aron the Divo of El Paso will perform a musical homage to Juan Gabriel as the event's grand finale.

Now in its third year, the cook-off has grown beyond a neighborhood gathering. Organizers note that attendees and contestants are expected from well outside the community, including Alamogordo — a sign, they say, that the event is becoming a regional destination.

item.title: PNM Executives Face Otero County Customers Today as NM Department of Justice Demands Answers on Billing Complaints
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — September 12, 2026 — The ongoing controversy over PNM electric bills in Otero County has escalated to the state level, with the New Mexico Department of Justice confirming this week that it has intervened directly with the utility after fielding rate-increase and billing complaints from customers across the state.

In a letter dated September 10 and signed by Mark Hayden, Division Director of the NMDOJ Utilities Unit, the agency acknowledged that it has received complaints from "many PNM customers" concerning invoice irregularities over the last two months statewide. According to Hayden, initial attempts by his office to resolve the matter with PNM by telephone and online inquiry were unsuccessful — prompting him to personally hand-deliver a letter to PNM management and then meet in person with PNM's legal counsel to discuss the issues.

A Consistent Pattern

The NMDOJ letter describes a consistent pattern in the complaints. Customers received emails from PNM stating the utility was unable to obtain a reading of their electric meter "due to unforeseen circumstances." The emails told customers that PNM had estimated their meter reading for the month using historical usage from the account, while cautioning that changes in usage and outside temperatures could affect the accuracy of the estimate.

The problem, according to the NMDOJ: those billing estimates have often been significantly higher than any previous bill the customer had ever received.

From a Facebook Group to the AG's Office

For many Alamogordo residents, the road to Santa Fe began much closer to home. Affected customers began comparing notes on the local Facebook page "City Watch Group – Alamogordo and Surrounding Areas," where they discovered the inflated estimated bills weren't isolated incidents — the same thing was happening to neighbors across the community. Katie Bevers Nichols is encouraging those that did not receive a written letter nor an email to contact the NMDOJ and let them know this was done with no formal notice as required. 

Local reporting on the issue helped connect residents with the right state agencies, directing them to the New Mexico Department of Justice, the Attorney General's office, and consumer protection channels. One Alamogordo complainant, in correspondence with the NMDOJ this week, disputed PNM's account of its own outreach, telling the agency that PNM never sent notices by mail to customers without email and that the utility "didn't do anything" until a local journalist contacted them directly.

It appears one individual's persistence in documenting and reporting the problem has now put the issue squarely on the state's radar — turning what many customers were told was a one-off billing hiccup into a formal, statewide inquiry.

What the State Is Demanding

The NMDOJ says PNM owes its customers three things: a detailed explanation of what happened, a plan for resolution by a certain date, and accurate billing for actual electrical consumption going forward.

"The NMDOJ is affording PNM an opportunity to resolve this matter before it takes further action," Hayden wrote, adding that the agency anticipates PNM will soon respond with a plan for resolution and that it will provide updates to keep complainants informed.

PNM Responds

Following the NMDOJ's intervention, PNM provided the following full statement to this publication in response to our media inquiry, delivered by PNM spokesperson Lisa Goodman:

"PNM has received the letter from the New Mexico Department of Justice, and we take the concerns raised by both our customers and the Department seriously.

We sincerely apologize for the confusion and frustration some of our customers experienced due to our meter reading staffing shortage. These shortages have caused some customers' bills to be delayed or estimated.

We want to assure customers that have received estimated bills that those bills will be reconciled when an actual meter reading is obtained, thus ensuring customers pay only for the electricity they actually use.

We recognize the inconvenience these issues have caused, and we are dedicated to providing customers with the time, flexibility, and support they need as we continue working to restore normal operations. For affected customers we have:

1. Put protections in place to ensure customers affected by delayed or estimated bills are not further impacted. This includes not charging late fees or disconnecting service for nonpayment.

2. We are offering payment extensions and flexible payment arrangements.

3. Financial assistance may also be available through the Good Neighbor Fund for eligible customers.

Again, we apologize for the issues we have caused. We want our customers to know we are working urgently to address the meter staffing challenges.

Customers with questions can visit PNM.com/BillingQuestions for additional information, answers to common questions, and details about available customer assistance resources or call us directly at 844-378-5792, M-F, 7:30am to 6pm."

The statement marks the utility's first public acknowledgment that a meter reading staffing shortage is behind the wave of delayed and estimated bills, and its first commitment that estimated bills will be reconciled against actual readings.

PNM at the Inkwell Today Until Noon

PNM representatives are in Alamogordo today, Saturday, September 12, 2026, hosting a community event at the Inkwell, running until noon. The event gives affected customers a chance to speak with the utility face to face about their bills.

Attendance interest has been modest so far, however, with only about 30 people signed up ahead of the event — a small showing given the volume of billing complaints circulating in local community groups. Customers with billing concerns still have time to stop by before noon today.

What Customers Should Do

PNM customers in Otero County who believe they have received inflated estimated bills are encouraged to attend today and or: 

• Keep copies of all bills and any "estimated reading" emails from PNM

• File a complaint with the New Mexico Department of Justice at nmdoj.gov

• Compare recent bills against the same billing period from prior years

This is a developing story. Updates will be published as the NMDOJ evaluates PNM's response and reconciled bills begin reaching customers and via further direct communications with complaintants and PNM executives. 

PNM should give money back to all those they severely overcharged instead of making customers find a way to make payments for PNM's mistakes.

item.title: Counseling Center, and Nadia Sikes Take Top Honors as Otero County Nonprofits "Hold It Together" at Third Annual Summit
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — The Sacramento Mountains Foundation capped its third annual Otero County Nonprofit Summit on Friday, September 11, with the presentation of $7,500 in cash awards, honoring the Counseling Center of Alamogordo as Nonprofit Organization of the Year and Nadia Sikes as Nonprofit Professional of the Year.

The Counseling Center received the $5,000 organization award, which recognizes an Otero County nonprofit whose people, programs, and stewardship set the standard for the sector. Sikes was presented the $2,500 professional award, given to an individual whose work, day in and day out, holds an organization and a community together. Winners were announced live at the close of the Summit, held at the CHRISTUS Southern New Mexico Conference Center on North Scenic Drive.

A Day Built Around the People Behind the Work

This year's theme, "Holding It Together: Sustaining and Leading the People Behind Otero County's Nonprofits," framed a full single-track day of keynotes, workshops, and working panels — all centered on one urgent question: how do the people who hold our nonprofits together sustain their energy over the long haul?

The room reflected the breadth of Otero County's nonprofit community. Organizations including 100% Otero, Thrive, COPE, and the Royal Angels were among those represented, spanning services from child and family wellbeing to crisis support to community outreach — a cross-section of the missions that serve the county every day.

Nationally Recognized Speakers

The day opened with a keynote from Beth Kanter, the internationally recognized author, speaker, and trainer whose bestselling book The Happy, Healthy Nonprofit has reshaped how the sector thinks about the wellbeing of the people who do the work. Kanter's morning session, "The Happy, Healthy Nonprofit: Where Resilience Meets Impact," explored burnout prevention and building cultures of wellbeing. She returned in the afternoon for a hands-on workshop, "From Ideas to Action: The Five F's for a Culture of Wellbeing," guiding attendees through practical, low-cost ways to build wellbeing into their organizations.

Edward "EJ" Wood IV, leadership speaker, author of The Shadow in the Silence, and founder of ENW Global Enterprises, followed with "Carry What Matters: Holding It Together When the Work Gets Heavy." Drawing on more than 16 years of military leadership experience, Wood challenged nonprofit executives and board members to examine what they are carrying, what they may be avoiding, and how meaningful service can turn into resentment when responsibility is concentrated in too few hands. "We may not get to choose every burden life places before us," Wood told the audience, "but we do get to decide who we become while carrying it."

Santa Fe-based leadership coach Zach Taylor led the late-morning session, "Building Strong Cultures at All Levels of an Organization: From Leadership to Volunteers," tackling what many call the hardest problem small organizations face — recruiting, keeping, and getting the best from the people who power the mission.

In the afternoon, Susan Decker, principal of Decker Consultants and senior governance consultant with BoardSource, presented "Building Trust and Accountability: The Board–Executive Partnership." Decker, whose clients have included the Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian, Ronald McDonald House Charities, and Make-A-Wish International, walked attendees through the trust, clarity, and mutual accountability essential to strong board–executive relationships.

The day closed with "Ask the Experts," a panel bringing all four speakers to one stage for audience questions, followed by the awards ceremony.

A Day That Belongs to the Sector

Admission to the Summit was free, with breakfast and lunch included — part of the Foundation's commitment to making the day accessible to organizations of every size and budget.

The Sacramento Mountains Foundation presents the Otero County Nonprofit Summit each year so that the people who lead, staff, and volunteer for the county's nonprofits have a day that is theirs: to learn, to compare notes, and to be recognized for work that rarely gets a spotlight.

For more information about the Sacramento Mountains Foundation, visit sacmtns.org.

item.title: El Paso Man Wanted on Rape, Drug Charges from Inn of the Mountain Gods Case
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — An El Paso, Texas man is wanted on a nationwide warrant charging him with second-degree criminal sexual penetration after he allegedly drugged and raped a woman at the Inn of the Mountain Gods on the Mescalero Apache Reservation.

Danny Rivera, 24, is wanted on the warrant, which was signed Aug. 12. He is charged with second-degree criminal sexual penetration resulting in personal injury and distribution of flunitrazepam, a benzodiazepine commonly associated with date rape.

New Mexico State Police Investigator Edward Garcia wrote in court documents that he enlisted the help of the FBI to identify Rivera from a selfie the victim allegedly took with him before the June 7 incident. Rivera was subsequently identified by the people he was sharing a hotel room with, his cousin and aunt, Garcia wrote.

The allegations

According to the woman's account detailed in court documents, she and a male friend went to the Inn of the Mountain Gods together, but she went to "The Game Room" alone, where she began talking to a man standing next to a casino machine watching another man play. She told him her 65-year-old boyfriend had ditched her, Garcia wrote.

The two went from the gaming room to a bar, and she took a selfie with the man while walking in a hallway at 10:03 p.m. — her last memory before waking up in the hospital attached to an IV line, Garcia wrote.

Her friend told investigators he had called her phone and a man with a Spanish accent answered, telling him to come get her and stating, in vulgar terms, that she had been sexually assaulted, Garcia wrote. When the friend called again later, a nurse answered. He went to the hospital and stayed with the woman until she was released.

Security footage

Garcia obtained security footage from the hotel and casino. Through the footage, he tracked the woman's movement from the gaming room to the bar with a man, then to an elevator, where she was having difficulty walking, Garcia wrote.

The footage showed her getting off the elevator on the seventh floor and going into a room with the man at 10:06 p.m. At 11:01 p.m., the man was seen carrying and dragging her out of the room, Garcia wrote.

The footage then showed her getting into the elevator with the man, who dragged her down part of a fourth-floor hallway before dropping her and walking away. A maid found her and radioed for help, Garcia wrote.

The evidence

A sexual assault examination nurse wrote in her report that the woman had vaginal bruising. At the hospital, a urine sample tested positive for benzodiazepine, a painkiller and sedative the woman said she did not take, Garcia wrote.

The woman was also covered in bruises on her biceps, left knee, both inner thighs and her left outer thigh, Garcia wrote.

A DNA report found the woman's dress tested positive for male DNA, according to court documents.

Rivera went to the El Paso Police Department on July 13 for an interview, where he declined to give a statement and asked for an attorney.

Anyone with information on Rivera's whereabouts is asked to contact New Mexico State Police, this is an ongoing investigation with an active nationwide warrant issued.

item.title: Friday Night Roundup: Roswell Runs Past Alamogordo; Tularosa, Grady Roll to Shutouts
item.description:
Alamogordo, Tiger Stadium- The Roswell Coyotes leaned on a punishing ground game and never trailed Friday night, pulling away from Alamogordo 56-26 in the district opener for both teams.

Roswell struck early and often. Luis Rodriguez broke loose for a 58-yard touchdown run just over two minutes into the game, and with 9:48 still showing in the first quarter the Coyotes led 7-0. Andruw Fuentez then found Danny Castro on a 38-yard scoring strike at the 5:42 mark to make it 14-0.

Alamogordo answered late in the opening frame. Qymani Patterson raced 36 yards for the Tigers' first touchdown, though the extra point missed, and Roswell carried a 14-6 lead into the second quarter.

The second period turned into a shootout. Fuentez added a 12-yard touchdown run at 9:37 to push the lead to 21-6, but the Tigers kept fighting — Samuel Strong ripped off a 35-yard scoring run, with Russell converting the extra point, to cut it to 21-13 with 8:06 before halftime. Fuentez responded again, this time from 45 yards out, restoring a 28-13 cushion. Alamogordo got the last word of the half when Tristan Bowman punched in a 4-yard touchdown as time expired, and the missed extra point left the score 28-19 at the break.

Any hopes of an Alamogordo comeback faded in the third quarter, when Roswell scored twice without an answer. Zeke Barrientos went 38 yards to paydirt with 6:29 to play in the period, and Rodriguez added his second long touchdown of the night — a 43-yard burst at 3:49 — to open a 42-19 lead heading to the fourth.

Patterson gave the Tigers a spark early in the final quarter with an 8-yard touchdown run to make it 42-26, but Roswell slammed the door. Danny Guevara scored from 9 yards out at 9:44, and Jonathan Ellis capped the scoring with a 4-yard touchdown run with 2:34 remaining.

The loss drops Alamogordo to 1-3 overall and 0-1 in district play. The Tigers travel to face Goddard next Friday.

item.title: Judge Dismisses Recall Petition Against Commissioner Burnett, Finds No Legal Duty per Existing Charter Ordinances to Answer Constituents
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — A district judge has dismissed a petition seeking a recall election against Alamogordo City Commissioner Stephen W. Burnett, ruling that the petitioner failed to establish enough evidence of probable cause on her claims of misconduct tied to the city's turbulent, two-year search for a city manager.

In a 22-page order filed September 9, Twelfth Judicial District Judge John P. Sugg rejected the petitioner Kim Murillo's allegations of misfeasance, malfeasance, and violation of oath of office, finding not enough evidence submitted that could prove Burnett acted with an improper or corrupt motive in any of the votes at the center of the dispute.

No Charter obligation to explain votes — or answer constituents

Perhaps the ruling's most consequential holding for Alamogordo residents: elected officials in the city have no legal duty to respond to constituent inquiries per the evidence submitted. 

Murillo's petition grew out of frustration that Burnett, her district's commissioner, agreed to answer her questions about the city manager hiring process and then never followed through. The court found that failure undisputed — but not unlawful. Because Murillo cited no authority within the Charter requiring a commissioner to respond to constituents, the court assumed none exists and treated Burnett's silence as a discretionary act.

Judge Sugg acknowledged the city's Code of Conduct requires officials to give constituents a fair opportunity to express concerns and grievances, but concluded nothing in the city's ordinances creates an obligation to answer every inquiry a commissioner receives. Drawing on the purposes behind the Speech and Debate Clauses of the state and federal constitutions — while suggesting they do not directly apply to city commissioners — the court reasoned that representatives are generally under no obligation to explain their votes, and that there is a difference between transparent government and a right to know an elected official's internal thinking.

"It is understandably frustrating," the judge wrote, that a representative promised to communicate and failed to do so — but nothing in the law presented compels such action.

The hiring saga behind the petition

The recall effort traces back to the resignation of City Manager Rick Holden in late 2024. Assistant City Manager Stephanie Hernandez served as acting manager while the commission ran two recruitment processes — one in-house, one through a national executive search firm. Hernandez was the only candidate to earn a passing score under the commission's own rubric in the first round, which was abandoned after then-Mayor Susan Payne described the process as "tainted" by commissioners' public comments about a candidate.

After Hernandez filed an EEOC inquiry against the city, the commission voted unanimously in March 2026 to offer her the permanent job with an admission the process was tainted. Contract talks stalled due to a demand to drop the EEOC inquiry, and in April the commission voted 4–3 — with Burnett in the majority — to instead accept Hernandez's one of two settlement proposals by Hernandez either pay  her $485,340.45 in backpay and ending her employment or issue her a contract as agreed for $360,000. Instead the majority offered her a back pay settlement and then offered a contract near half million to Stockwell together costing the city nearly $1 million dollars that was avoidable but per the judge, Burnett not required to explain. 

Two months later, the commission voted 5–2 to hire Robert Stockwell, who had not applied through either recruitment process. Burnett voted in favor. Murillo argued the reversal on Hernandez, the Stockwell hire, and alleged Open Meetings Act violations amounted to recallable misconduct.

Patillo and Rardin drove the Stockwell hire, court finds and may have opened a door to malfeasance. 

While the order clears Burnett, its findings place the recruitment of Stockwell squarely with two other officials: Commissioner Baxter Patillo and Mayor Pro-Tem Joshua Rardin. The court found the pair had been actively recruiting Stockwell since the initial hiring process began, and that Patillo circulated a proposed contract to the full commission three days before the June 15 special meeting at which Stockwell was interviewed and hired — legwork Patillo himself described in emails as "my solo legwork."

The court found no evidence Burnett played any role in recruiting Stockwell or made any private agreement on how to vote. Whether the ruling's findings fuel further political fallout for the other two commissioners who orchestrated the hire is a question the order does not answer — a recall against any official would require its own showing of probable cause under the same demanding standard Murillo's petition failed to meet specific to Burnett. 

Claims that Burnett violated the city's Code of Conduct by contacting zoo and golf course employees directly, and that he used his position to advance his sister-in-law's Local Economic Development Act application, also failed — the former for lack of admissible evidence beyond hearsay, the latter because the conduct at issue occurred in 2025, during Burnett's prior term, and recall grounds are limited to the current term.

Citing New Mexico Supreme Court precedent, Judge Sugg stressed that recall is available "for cause, and not recall at will," and that the standard must be limited to avoid employing recall for harassment or purely political purposes.

Attorney: stronger case exists against other commissioners

An attorney who reviewed the court record said the findings point to a far stronger case against Patillo and Rardin than the one brought against Burnett, and contended that additional evidence of Open Meetings Act violations exists in the city's own files — including what the attorney described as admissions of prior misconduct — that was never presented at the July 29 probable cause hearing. That evidence was not in the record before Judge Sugg.

The same attorney questioned the court's conclusion that no law obligates officials to respond to constituents, pointing to the body of state and federal transparency requirements imposed on government at every level.

The failure, the attorney argued, may lie not in the law itself but in the citations the petition failed to put before the court — a reading the order arguably invites, since Judge Sugg rested that holding expressly on Murillo's failure to cite authority, citing State v. Casares for the proposition that a court assumes no authority exists where none is offered.

Where the attorney has a real point: New Mexico's IPRA does impose an enforceable duty with deadlines — a custodian must respond to a written records request within 15 days, NMSA 1978 § 14-2-8(D), with damages and fees available under § 14-2-12. If Murillo's inquiries had been framed and cited as IPRA requests, there'd have been more state actual statutory authority in front of the court rather than the limited authority of the weak city charter. Same for OMA's enforcement provisions at § 10-15-3. That's the gap — not a duty to answer emails, but a duty to produce records that the petition never invoked may have been the missing component to the Murillo effort. 

"A small setback"

Murillo said she was disappointed in the ruling but “encouraged by what she has seen from Burnett since, noting he attended a recent community forum and appears more engaged with the district.”

She acknowledged Burnett's was the weaker of the cases she could have brought, but said the court affirmed points that will help future efforts and did not reflect well on Patillo or Rardin.

Murillo said her goal “is a government responsive to the people, and that rules holding political leadership accountable to constituents need tightening.”  She said she intends “to keep pressing for transparency and views the dismissal as a small setback in a larger effort.”

item.title: Save the Date Oct 17, 2026 Corks & Shells Returns: Thrive's Wine and Pistachio Festival Grows in Year Two
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — When Thrive in Southern New Mexico launched the Corks & Shells Wine & Pistachio Festival last October, organizers called it a tradition in the making and promised it would return to Alameda Park on the third weekend of every October. They are keeping that promise. The second annual Corks & Shells Wine Festival is set for Saturday, Oct. 17, from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., and by most measures it will be bigger than the first.

The inaugural festival on Oct. 18, 2025, was pitched as a celebration of the two crops that define the Tularosa Basin's agricultural identity — grapes and pistachios — wrapped around a fundraiser for Thrive, the Alamogordo nonprofit formerly known as the United Way of Otero County that channels support to regional agencies working on food insecurity, education, mental health and child advocacy.

Four regional producers poured at that first event: Heart of the Desert, Noisy Water Winery, Ruidoso Fine Wine & Art and Tularosa Vineyards. More than two dozen vendors set up in the park with handcrafted goods, fashion and local services, among them Alamogordo MainStreet, Gerald Champion Regional Medical Center and Southern NM Family Services. Acoustic group Yankee Lima, DJ Dale Rulbe and Dzak Sukarno handled the entertainment, and a "Witchy Pumpkin" paint-and-sip session gave attendees a creative break between tastings.

Advance tickets were $15, gate admission $20, with $5 designated driver tickets and free entry for guests under 21. In partnership with the Kiwanis Club of Alamogordo, Thrive ran a shoe drive for local youth alongside the festival, rewarding donors of new shoes with a pizza gift certificate. Executive Director Michelle Gill, who led the event, framed it as a way to raise both funds and awareness for families, seniors, underserved youth and those in need of rehabilitation services. At the time, Thrive reported having distributed more than $348,000 to regional agencies.

The wine tent has already sold out of vendor slots — the lineup for Oct. 17 is set.

The most visible change is the pour list. Six wineries are featured for 2026, up from four, and the roster reaches well beyond the basin: Rio Grande Winery, Noisy Water Winery & Cellars, Vintage United, Sheehan Winery, Black Range Vineyards of Hillsboro, and D.H. Lescombes Family Vineyards of Deming, whose brands include St. Clair, 6.3.1, Soleil Mimosa and Vines de los Muertos. Noisy Water is the lone returning name from the 2025 lineup. Wine vendor registration is listed as sold out on the event page.

Ticketing has also moved. Last year's tickets sold through Thrive's own website; this year the festival is using the RunSignup/TicketSignup platform, and pricing has been simplified to a single $20 general admission ticket, with a small processing fee added online. There is no separate advance discount or designated driver tier listed, and under-21 admission remains free — though organizers stress that every attendee, including children, must hold a ticket. Visit Alamogordo has come on as a partner.

Food trucks, pistachio growers, arts and crafts vendors and cottage bakers will fill out the grounds again, with live music through the afternoon. Taquero Rey is the first announced food truck and Enchanted Treasures 575 is among the confirmed craft vendors. Vendor registration for food trucks ($150) and arts, crafts and cottage bakers ($50) stays open through Sept. 30, so the vendor list will keep growing over the next two weeks.

item.title: Off-Road Triathlon's Biggest Race Comes to Ruidoso for XTERRA's 30th Anniversary
item.description:
RUIDOSO, N.M. — Less than a month from now, this mountain village of roughly 8,000 people will host the biggest event in off-road triathlon. The XTERRA World Championship runs October 8–11, 2026, centered on Grindstone Lake and Ruidoso's trail system, at over 6,900 feet in the Lincoln National Forest.

How many are coming

XTERRA U.S. Tour Manager Steve Andrus has estimated the championship will draw between 1,000 and 1,500 athletes plus their families and friends, with as many as 7,000 visitors in total. Most arrive from outside the state — Mayor Lynn Crawford has said roughly 97% of visitors for the village's new endurance events are first-timers to the community, coming from around the world rather than just Texas and Arizona.

Athletes qualify by winning or placing highly in their age group at World Tour events. Beginning in 2026, athletes aged 18–19 race for their world title at the Youth World Championship in a sprint format rather than the full distance.

The course

Three championship races will be contested across the Elite, Age Group and Youth divisions, with the full-distance triathlon set for October 10.

The full distance is a 1.5K swim in Grindstone Lake, a 27K mountain bike leg with nearly 2,950 feet of climbing across Grindstone Mesa, and a 10K trail run through pine forest. Swimmers exit between two 750-meter laps, an XTERRA tradition. The run finishes at Wingfield Park in the heart of town. XTERRA's original announcement described a 30K bike leg, so expect final distances to firm up closer to race day. October averages around 63°F locally.

A sport born on a beach in Maui

The first race was held November 3, 1996, under the name Aquaterra, with 123 athletes in Wailea, Maui — won by Jimmy Riccitello and Michellie Jones. It aired on Fox Sports Net, and the format spread quickly; the series now counts more than 50,000 competitors across 50-plus countries.The race moved from Maui's south shore to Kapalua in 2011

, and Maui hosted the world championship for 25 straight years before the event relocated to Molveno in the Italian Dolomites in 2022. The 2025 edition in Molveno closed out a four-year Italian run. Ruidoso is only the fourth venue in the championship's history.

What it means for the region

The timing matters locally. Burn scars from the 2024 South Fork and Salt fires produced destructive flooding in both the 2024 and 2025 monsoon seasons, shuttering Ruidoso Downs Racetrack — one of the area's main economic engines — which announced it would stay closed through 2026. Flooding in July 2025 killed three people and damaged homes and businesses.

Village leaders have leaned hard into endurance tourism as a replacement draw. Ruidoso hosted New Mexico's first IRONMAN-branded race, the IRONMAN 70.3 Ruidoso, on July 11–12 this year, and has committed to the XTERRA World Championship for three consecutive years, 2026 through 2028. Crawford called the selection "a tremendous honor for our mountain community."

For visitors

Expect peak lodging demand and busy restaurants, with athletes arriving mid-week for check-in and training. Beyond the course, the area offers Fort Stanton and Lincoln historic sites, Smokey Bear Historical Park, and the Wingfield Heritage House Museum. Ruidoso was also named the No. 1 Best Small Town Cultural Scene in the 2026 USA TODAY 10Best Readers' Choice Awards, its second straight year with the honor.

Race-week road closures and spectator information are typically posted through the Village of Ruidoso and Discover Ruidoso ahead of the event.

item.title: Recall Organizer Vows to Press On After Judge Rejects Petition Against Commissioner Burnett
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — A district judge has rejected a petition to recall Alamogordo City Commissioner Stephen Burnett, finding a lack of probable cause, but the resident leading the effort says the case was only the beginning.

Kim White Owl Murillo, who organized the recall, told KALH Radio host Anthony Lucero in a phone interview that the group will not appeal the ruling. Instead, she said, the evidence brought to light during the proceedings will be used to support possible cases against other members of the commission.

"It was disappointing news, but a lot of good things have come out of it," Murillo said. "This was our first case, but it brought out a lot of things that the commissioners have been doing."

Murillo described Burnett, who represents District 2, as "the low fruit on the tree."

Murillo said she accepts the outcome and believes the judge took care with the case despite carrying a heavy criminal docket after the hearing. She declined to detail why the group chose not to appeal, citing "various reasons."

What troubled her most, she said, was the court's finding that Burnett has no obligation to explain his decisions to constituents.

"So now they're gonna think, oh, we can just do what we want," Murillo said. But she argued that commissioners often reveal their reasoning when residents question them directly. "When they respond, they don't know to cover up. They just talk."

She urged residents to "start being detectives" by watching commission decisions closely and pressing officials for explanations.

Murillo tied the recall effort to the commission's decision to hire Robert Stockwell as city manager and part ways with former Acting City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez, a move she said has left a "huge void" at City Hall.

"We're not gonna get things done, because they're going way back," she said, adding that some are now trying to discredit Hernandez. Of Stockwell, a former Alamogordo city manager who returned to the post this summer, she said, "He's not living in 2026. He's living in the nineties."

Murillo pointed to the future of Bonita Lake as an early measure of whether public pressure is working. She said Burnett attended a Sept. 1 community forum on the lake hosted by 2nd Life Media, where residents made clear they oppose closing it.

If Burnett supports fencing off the lake when the issue comes before the commission Sept. 22, Murillo said, he will be "going against the voters' will" and should be called out. If he instead works to keep it open, she said, "then we're influencing him."

Murillo said the group has gathered more evidence concerning two other commissioners, whom she declined to name, and is looking for residents willing to step forward and take a case to court. She said the group is planning its strategy and may hold public meetings.

She encouraged residents to share their thoughts and suggest potential petitioners through the group's Facebook page, Alamogordo Voters for Accountability.

"You've got a whole team now who's willing to step in and help you out," she said.

Murillo closed by praising residents who have spoken out, particularly about Bonita Lake. "I'm just so proud of Alamogordo citizens," she said.

item.title: EDITORIAL: Alamogordo's Charter Protects Officials, Not Citizens. Voters Should Rewrite It
item.description:
When a district judge threw out the recall petition against City Commissioner Stephen Burnett, the most troubling part of the ruling wasn't the outcome. It was the reasoning. Under Alamogordo's existing charter and ordinances, the court found, an elected commissioner has no legal duty to answer to the constituents who put him in office.

Read that again. The people's representatives are not required to explain themselves to the people.

That is not a failure of one judge or one commissioner. It is a failure of the document that governs this city, and it is one Alamogordo voters have the power to fix.

Alamogordo's charter was adopted in 1983. It has been amended a handful of times since, mostly on procedural matters such as how runoff elections work. It sets up a commission-manager government in which six commissioners and a mayor set policy and hire a city manager to run daily operations.

What the charter does not do is give residents meaningful tools to hold that commission accountable between elections. Recall is the only real remedy, and in New Mexico it is a narrow one. Petitioners must convince a judge there is probable cause of legal misconduct. Voting against the public's clearly stated wishes, refusing to explain a decision, or making costly choices behind closed doors does not clear that bar.

The past year has shown what that gap looks like in practice.

This spring, weeks after voting unanimously to negotiate a contract with Acting City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez, the commission reversed course on a 4-3 vote and accepted a taxpayer-funded settlement to push her out. It then installed Robert Stockwell, a former city manager the commission fired in 1997 and declined to rehire in 2016. The hiring process itself is now the subject of a lawsuit alleging Open Meetings Act violations.

Residents asked why. Many are still waiting for an answer, and under the charter as the court has read it, they may never get one.

Now the fate of Bonita Lake, a place residents have told commissioners in no uncertain terms they want kept open, is headed to a vote on Sept. 22. Citizens deserve to know that whatever commissioners decide, they will be obligated to say why.

Term limits. A commission with no ceiling on service invites entrenchment. Long-tenured blocs build relationships with insiders, not with the broader public, and incumbency makes them hard to dislodge. Limiting commissioners to two consecutive terms would bring in fresh perspectives, loosen the grip of any single faction, and remind officeholders that their seats belong to the voters, not to them.

A duty to respond. The charter should require commissioners to publicly explain their votes on major decisions such as hiring or firing a city manager, approving settlements, and closing or selling public assets. It should also set a reasonable deadline for commissioners to respond to written questions from constituents. Accountability should not depend on whether an official feels like talking.

Critics of term limits argue that voters can already remove officials at the ballot box, and that forcing out experienced commissioners sacrifices institutional knowledge. Those are fair points. But ballot-box accountability works only when voters have full information, and a commission with no duty to explain itself withholds exactly that. As for institutional knowledge, this city has just watched that phrase used to justify rehiring a manager who was fired a generation ago.

Others may worry that a response requirement would bog down city business. A few paragraphs explaining a major vote is not a burden. It is the job.

The charter gives voters a path to amend it themselves. A petition signed by enough qualified voters, based on recent city election turnout, can place amendments before the electorate. Residents do not need the commission's permission, and they should not wait for it.

The recall effort against Commissioner Burnett did not succeed in court. But it succeeded in exposing the real problem. Alamogordo's government answers to a charter that asks too little of the people in power. It is time for the people to ask for more, and to write it down.

Stay tuned a process exists, the organization begins…

item.title: Thrive Rallies Volunteers for Day of Caring, Gears Up for Corks and Shells Wine Festival
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — More than 160 volunteers will fan out across Alamogordo and Otero County this Friday, Sept. 18, for Thrive in Southern New Mexico's annual Day of Caring, a local tradition now in its 36th year.

Volunteers will work on 44 homes throughout the county, according to Michelle Gill of Thrive. Many of this year's volunteers come from Holloman Air Force Base and several community financial institutions.

"It should be a great day," Gill said.

The Day of Caring serves residents who are over 65, have a disability or are veterans. Volunteers handle outdoor work only, including minor yard work, debris removal, painting and tree trimming.

"It just is a great opportunity for people that need a little bit of a helping hand with some yard work and cleanup," Gill said.

Crews will start at about 8 a.m. and work until around noon. Volunteers will then gather in the atrium at First National Bank to share feedback and enjoy a lunch provided by Thrive.

The program began under United Way and is now run by Thrive. Organizing it takes months of planning. Thrive divides Alamogordo and Otero County into six regions, each with six to eight homes. Zone leaders contact each homeowner and make a visit before the workday so crews arrive with the right equipment.

"It's quite a feat to get this organized and get people where they're supposed to be, and to try to take care of as many people as we can within the limited amount of time that we have," Gill said.

She said the event reflects the strength of community pride in Alamogordo. "Sometimes we get lost in the doom and gloom stories, and there really are great people that are doing great things and making a huge impact in people's lives," she said.

Gill asked residents who spot volunteers on Friday to "give them a honk and a wave and let them know that they're appreciated."

Thrive's next big event is the Corks and Shells Wine Festival, set for Saturday, Oct. 17, at Alameda Park. Now in its third year, the festival will be held on the third Saturday of October going forward.

Six wineries from around the region will take part. Thrive has capped the number of wineries at six so the event doesn't become oversaturated and every guest can enjoy the day, Gill said. The festival will also feature food trucks, art and craft vendors, and a paint-in.

Gill said she hopes the festival brings back the feel of the Cottonwood Festival of years past.

Tickets are on sale now and include a wine glass. Guests can sample from the visiting wineries and buy bottles to take home.

Tickets, art and craft vendor sign-ups, and food truck applications for Corks and Shells are available at letsthrivenm.org. item.title: Eyes on the Road: Dr. Stephanie Hernandez on Why Alamogordo Turned to Flock Cameras
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Alamogordo Town News and KALHRadio.org have introduced a new weekly segment, "The Doctor Is In," featuring former Alamogordo City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez. The series will offer insights into governance, business, nonprofit work and public policy.

In the debut episode, Hernandez, who led the effort to bring Flock license plate reader (LPR) cameras to Alamogordo, walked listeners through why the city pursued the technology, the safeguards it put in place, and the results she saw before leaving her post.

A Response to Rising Property Crime and Staffing Shortages

Hernandez said the push began in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, when property crime rose through 2022 and 2023. City staff and the City Commission received numerous complaints about stolen property, including vehicles.

At the same time, the Alamogordo Police Department was stretched thin. According to Hernandez, APD had only 37 certified officers as of July 2023.

Hernandez said she and Alamogordo Police Chief David Kunihiro had to look at long-term solutions and better tools. "That's when we agreed to look at Flock," she said.

After research and a series of meetings, the proposal went before the City Commission in December 2024. Representatives from Flock presented alongside Las Cruces Police Chief Jeremy Story, who shared his department's experience using license plate readers and real-time crime technology. Hernandez said APD was handling roughly 83 stolen vehicle cases a year at the time. The commission responded positively, and the city moved forward.

Privacy Guardrails

Hernandez said privacy was discussed at length before the system was adopted, and the city built in several limits:

• Restricted access: Only APD command staff, or personnel the police chief deemed necessary for a specific investigation, could access the system.

• Minimal data retention: The city deliberately kept retention periods as short as possible.

• No tracking of residents: "We were not creating records for citizens' whereabouts," Hernandez said.

• No facial recognition: The cameras capture vehicle information only.

• Lawful use: Hernandez noted the city already operated cameras at public facilities, including parks, and those systems were integrated with Flock to improve effectiveness.

"We made sure we had tight controls and spent a lot of time limiting who had access, how it could be used, and how much information would be retained," she said.

How It Was Funded

Hernandez said she identified highly restricted funding sources that could not legally be spent on roads or infrastructure. General fund dollars were also used. She described balancing restricted and unrestricted funds as a core part of her responsibility to the public.

Acknowledging Public Concerns

Hernandez said residents' concerns about surveillance are valid, but she urged perspective. She pointed out that people are routinely recorded by business security cameras, home doorbell cameras and cell phones, often without knowing it, and that private owners can use that footage for virtually any purpose. By contrast, she said, the city's system operated under defined rules.

Transparency and Results

According to Hernandez, Flock came before the City Commission at least four times. APD shared information about the program on its social media pages, and the program drew local and statewide media coverage.

"I was pleased with the results at the time that I left," Hernandez said. "It was recovering stolen vehicles and solving crimes."

She closed the segment with a message to listeners: "Remember, representation starts with participation, so stay engaged."
